item.title: Stripes of the Week: Week 8 at Auburn
item.description: Several LSU players had performances worthy of stripes, but with only three picks each, only six can earn honors this week.
item.content:encoded:
After eight weeks, we probably do not need to make the NHL “Three Stars of the Week” comparison anymore, so here is how David Billiot Jr. and I snake-drafted our Stripes of the Week for our podcast, Geaux Deep Dive, for Week 8. After such a dominating win, it was difficult to pick just three players each this week.

Three Stripes: Sam Leavitt (Zach), Jackson Harris (David)

On a bad hamstring, Sam Leavitt, for the second week in a row, earns three stripes. The back-to-back honors were enough to push him one stripe ahead of Deuce Geralds for the season lead heading into the bye week. It is deserved. Over the past two weeks, Leavitt has completed 63 of his 83 pass attempts for 676 yards and seven touchdowns while carrying the ball 12 times for 65 yards and a touchdown. Over the course of the season, it has kind of been a tale of two tendencies for Leavitt. Early in the season, it felt like he was looking to run too much. Then he hurt his hamstring and was forced to stay and become more of a pocket passer. This week, even with the injury, we saw the most complete version (despite one nearly costly decision) of Sam Leavitt, going 32-of-45 for 387 yards and three touchdowns in the air, with eight carries for 54 yards and a touchdown on the ground. The important thing for Leavitt now is to keep up the elite play and rest that hamstring during the bye week.

To continue with the theme of fast risers up the Stripes standings, Jackson Harris elevates his two stripes from last week to three this week thanks to his nine catches for 178 yards and two touchdowns. 178 yards is the highest mark by an LSU receiver since Malik Nabers’ 239 yards in 2023 Week 3 at Mississippi State. With defenses starting to focus more on Winston Watkins Jr. after his performances to start the season, along with Trey’Dez Green going down with an injury, Harris has thrust his name into the conversation for one of the best wide receivers in the SEC.

Two Stripes: Jordan Ross (David), PJ Woodland (Zach)

Jordan Ross earned stripes for the second week in a row as well, and he arguably could have been in the three-stripe slot once again. Ross recorded four total tackles and two sacks, along with one pass deflection. The conversation around how good this LSU pass rush has been this season primarily focused on Princewill Umanmielen and Deuce Geralds, but after Princewill missed the majority of the game against Mississippi State, Ross stepped up. With Princewill having returned, the two formed a wrecking crew against Auburn, with three of the team’s seven sacks. If both EDGE rushers can stay healthy and perform as they did at Auburn, opposing defenses will have more than their hands full.

This pick could have gone to either PJ Woodland or DJ Pickett, and it probably should have gone to Pickett, but week after week Woodland continues to impress me with his hustle and grit. For a corner, leading the team in tackles without giving up any big plays shows a ton of grit and hustle. Woodland had nine total tackles, seven of which were solo, and one pass broken up. As the rest of the team continues to improve each week, so too does the cornerback duo of Woodland and Pickett.

One Stripe: Trey’Dez Green (Zach), Davhon Keys (David)

It would have been easy for Trey’Dez Green to just sit out until after the bye week and return for Alabama. It would have been just as easy for him to return this week, play minimal snaps, and just run as a decoy. Green took the gritty route and played the majority of the meaningful snaps in this game coming off the injury. Green, according to Lane Kiffin, only came out because Auburn kept trying to hip-drop tackle him late in the game. That grit from Green came in the form of five catches for 50 yards and one touchdown. Green coming back, with Jackson Harris emerging as an elite option, is going to cause nightmares for defensive coordinators trying to decide who they should key in on between Green, Harris and Watkins. Even if you do find a way to cover those three, LSU still has an abundance of talent they can look to after those guys to make defenses pay. The point is, while the offense was successful without Green, he just adds another dynamic weapon to the SEC’s top offense.

In games like this, we tend to look deep to find players who may not always be at the forefront of everyone’s mind to give them some deserved recognition. We did not have to look far this week. Davhon Keys breaks into the stripes list with seven tackles and a sack. It has been a bit of a winding road since he replaced the injured Whit Weeks, but Keys keeps learning and blossoming into a better player as the season goes on. With Weeks’ return on the horizon, Keys may see less playing time, but at the very least, Kiffin and Blake Baker know they can count on Keys to make some plays when he is called on.

Honorable Mention:

Dilin Jones: 24 carries, 94 yards, 1 touchdown, 4 catches, 27 yards
Aliou Bah: Second-highest-graded offensive lineman by PFF
DJ Pickett: 2 tackles, 1 tackle for a loss, 2 passes broken up
TJ Dottery: 6 tackles, 1 sack
Princewill Umanmielen: 5 tackles, 1 sack

item.title: 4 Cowboys players or things to buy or sell vs the Eagles
item.description: How confident are you feeling?
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys head to Philadelphia for a Monday night divisional matchup that could have major implications for the NFC East. Dallas has lost two straight games, and while there are still plenty of playmakers on offense, the team has struggled to put everything together. The Eagles are dealing with their own offensive problems after losing Jalen Hurts for the season, and are hoping their defense steps up.

Buy: Javonte Williams

If the Cowboys want to make life easier for Dak Prescott, the best place to start is with Javonte Williams. Dallas has leaned heavily on its passing game this season, but the offense has become increasingly predictable as the running game has struggled to find consistency. Williams deserves more opportunities to change that.

Through six games, Williams has carried the ball 85 times for 317 yards and seven rushing touchdowns, averaging 3.7 yards per attempt. He has also contributed 19 receptions for 103 yards and a receiving touchdown. Though his rushing average isn’t particularly impressive, his touchdown production shows Dallas has found a player it can trust when it gets close to the goal line.

There has been some discussion about Philadelphia’s susceptibility to I-formation, suggesting balance is the best way to attack this defense, but really Dallas needs to improve its rushing production, and Williams has already shown he can finish drives.

The Cowboys’ offensive line has struggled to create consistent running lanes, so this is not simply a matter of handing Williams the ball and expecting a breakout. Still, more carries would give Dallas a better chance to establish rhythm, keep the Eagles’ pass rush honest and avoid putting the entire offense on Prescott’s shoulders.

Williams is not guaranteed to have a huge game against a talented middle, but the Cowboys need to find out what their running game can do when they commit to it. Seven rushing touchdowns through six games is a good reason to keep feeding him.

Sell: The Cowboys’ passing game against Philadelphia’s defense

The Cowboys’ passing attack has plenty of talent, but this is a difficult week to expect a quick turnaround. Philadelphia has the personnel to make Prescott uncomfortable, especially if Dallas cannot establish the run or improve its protection.

Prescott has thrown four interceptions over the past two games, tied for the most in the NFL over that span. Against the blitz during those two games, he has completed just 52.6% of his passes without a touchdown, posting a 67.2 passer rating. Those numbers are a scary heading into a matchup against a defense that can challenge receivers on the outside and create problems in the middle of the field.

Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean are important pieces of that secondary, and Jalen Carter can disrupt an offense from the interior. Philadelphia also has a deep group of defensive contributors, including linebacker Zack Baun and run-stopper Jordan Davis, but edge rusher Nolan Smith will miss the game.

The Eagles have not been overwhelming in every pass-rush metric, so Dallas should have opportunities if the offensive line holds up. But the Cowboys have not earned the benefit of the doubt after two consecutive losses in which the offense struggled to sustain its production.

Prescott’s recent turnovers are especially glaring because Dallas cannot afford to give Philadelphia extra possessions in a divisional game. Until the Cowboys show they can handle pressure and take care of the football, the passing game is a sell against this Eagles defense.

Buy: Joey Porter Jr.

While the Cowboys’ defense has struggled to create turnovers, Joey Porter Jr. has given the secondary a reason for optimism. His physical style of coverage and ability to stay tight to receivers make him an important piece of a defense that needs more consistent playmaking.

Porter is particularly valuable heading into Monday night’s matchup because Philadelphia’s passing game is adjusting to life without Jalen Hurts. With Tanner McKee taking over at quarterback, the Cowboys need their cornerbacks to challenge receivers at the line of scrimmage, contest throws and make the Eagles work for every completion. Porter has the size and physicality to make those matchups uncomfortable.

Of course, good coverage only goes so far if the pass rush cannot pressure the quarterback. The Dallas pass rush has left the defensive backs to cover for extended stretches. That has contributed to the unit’s inability to consistently finish plays, even when the coverage is competitive.

Porter is a buy because he gives Dallas a potential building block in the secondary, not because one cornerback can fix the defense by himself. If the Cowboys can pair his coverage with more pressure up front, they have a better chance of forcing McKee into mistakes and creating the takeaways that have been missing.

Sell: The pass protection

The Cowboys’ offensive line has to give Dak Prescott more time to operate, because the pressure he has faced over the last two games has helped derail an offense that was previously one of the team’s biggest strengths.

Dallas has scored just 29 points combined in its last two games, and Prescott’s protection has been a significant concern as opposing defenses have disrupted the passing game. The Cowboys have allowed six sacks through six games, but the bigger issue has been the pressure and hurried decisions that prevent Prescott from getting through his progressions and finding CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens downfield.

The matchup against Philadelphia offers a potential reprieve, but it is hardly a reason to relax. The Eagles have recorded eight sacks this season, and Jalen Carter remains a disruptive presence on the interior. Philadelphia hasn’t consistently generated pressure with its standard four-man rush, but Dallas still needs to communicate well up front and keep Carter from collapsing the pocket. If the Eagles bring extra rushers, Prescott must have enough time and reliable outlets to punish them.

Dallas’ tackles, Tyler Guyton and Terence Steele, need to hold up on the edges, while the interior must keep Carter from disrupting the play’s timing. Until the Cowboys show they can consistently keep Prescott comfortable in the pocket, the offensive line remains a concern heading into Monday night.

item.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints loss to the Steelers
item.description: Saints run game beheaded in France
item.content:encoded:
The Good: Chase Young and Carl Granderson

The Saints pair of pass rushers was able to constantly put pressure on Steelers QB Aaron Rodgers on Sunday. Combining for 3 sacks, Granderson and Young are proving to be one of the better pass-rushing duos in the NFL. They rank 1st in the league for a duo with a combined 12.5 sacks, just ahead of the Texans Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter (11.5), and this is even with Granderson missing a game. Granderson has gotten 1.5 sacks in each of the last three games and is well on his way to his first career double digit sack season. The Saints took a risk investing long term in Chase Young given his injury history, but that risk has paid off in a big way, as the former second overall pick is looking every bit the player that warranted that pick with 17 sacks in his last 19 games.

The Bad: Rushing Offense

The Saints rushing offense hit a new low in Paris which is saying a lot given how poor it has been all year. The Saints ran 17 times for 18 yards, with the leading rusher being Tyler Shough with 3 carries for 7 yards. Alvin Kamara (3.0 ypc) and Kendre Miller (2.8 ypc) rank 37th and 39th respectively in terms of yards per carry among the 41 running backs in the NFL with 40+ carries. Prize free agent Travis Etienne Jr. has been out since Week 3 and was averaging 4.3 yards per carry before he went down. He is eligible to come off IR after the bye week, but even he won’t be enough to save the Saints ground game. The fact is they cannot block well up front as the offensive line is both banged up and also just not very good at run blocking. This was the fourth game this year where their leading rusher was held to 30 yards or fewer, and they have only eclipsed 100 yards as a team twice. Just adding a better running back will help a bit but will not fix the main cause of the Saints problems on the ground, and fixing the ground game should be arguably their highest priority in the offseason.

The Ugly: Finishing long drives

The Saints had four drives of 11+ plays on Sunday and only got points out of one of them. They opened with an 11-play drive that got to the Steelers 43-yard line before stalling due to penalties and being forced to punt but would go on to score on each of their next two drives which tied the game at 10. In the second half however, they had a 14-play drive that ended in a red zone interception, and an 11-play drive that ended in a missed 52-yard field goal. If they convert on each of those two drives, they are at least tied and have the ball with 7:04 left in the fourth quarter, and at best have a four-point lead and make the Steelers have to get in the end zone on their final drive. Before this game, the Saints had been good at finishing in the red zone, as this was Shough’s first red zone interception of his career, so let’s hope this is not a sign of things to come but just a one game anomaly.

item.title: Seahawks Droppings: Seattle destroys the Kansas City Chiefs, puts NFL on notice
item.description: With their backs against the wall, the Seahawks finally show up and make the Chiefs look like pretenders.
item.content:encoded:
I almost made the headline “Anthony Bradford’s return kickstarts Seahawks offense”, and that wouldn’t have been a lie. Finally, the 2026 Seattle Seahawks played a complete game, looking absolutely dominant in a 20-3 shellacking of the previously unbeaten Kansas City Chiefs on the same day that the San Francisco 49ers lost to the Atlanta Falcons. Talk about a perfect way to cap the weekend…in those beautiful throwback jerseys nonetheless!

All season long, the story has been the offense’s struggles marring elite defensive performances. We still got a goofy Sam Darnold pick just before the half, otherwise the score could’ve been even worse. No worries, the Seahawks defense stepped up in a big way holding former Seattle RB Kenneth Walker III to just 36 yards rushing. Meanwhile, Seattle ran for 153 yards and put up over 400 yards of offense. The mini bye was good to the Seahawks. 

Seahawks Droppings

  • Seattle muzzled K9 and harassed Patrick Mahomes all game. Walker was one of the leading rushers in the NFL, but had no room to bounce outside against the Seahawks. They only sacked Mahomes one time, but kept him to 19/33 for 165 yards passing and 1 INT. The Chiefs never reached the red zone…maybe that’s a good thing considering the defense’s struggles in that area. Regardless, that defensive performance was exquisite and Mike Macdonald should take a bow. 
  • Nick Emmanwori is a cheat code. Looking at his stats won’t tell the entire story. He’s been used all over the field this season, showing out as both a pass-rusher and coverage player. Emmanwori’s pressure on Mahomes directly resulted in Ty Okada’s interception. Later in the game, he was matched up one-on-one with speedster Xavier Worthy. No problem as Emmanwori stayed with him step for step on a deep ball that resulted in an incompletion. Sometimes I forget that he’s just 22 years old and that he missed all of training camp. Emmanwori will keep getting better, which is a scary thought for the rest of the NFL. 
  • Sam Darnold was dropping dimes. The interception was terrible, I’ll just get that out of the way. Those two deep throws to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, though? Beautiful. Sam made huge plays with his legs today as well, getting some key first downs. If he plays games like he did today, the Seahawks will win a lot more games this season. 
  • Jaxon Smith-Njigba is unstoppable. Literally. JSN reeled in 9 catches for 150 yards and 1 TD. He had those two huge aforementioned deep passes to go along with crossers over the middle. Credit Brian Fleury for finding ways to get JSN open and Darnold for finding him. Rashid Shaheed injured his knee and didn’t play in the second half. That will be something to monitor, but JSN will still get his. 
  • Seattle’s run game showed up. Emmanuel Wilson ran hard, gaining 100 yards on 24 carries with a game-clinching late TD. George Holani had a key third down conversion as well. Reinforcements should be on the way as Zach Charbonnet could make his season debut in Week 8 and Jadarian Price will be eligible to return from IR as well. That would give the run game even more juice which will in turn help the pass game. 
  • No sacks on Darnold. Is it a coincidence that in the week Anthony Bradford returns, Seattle rushes for a bunch of yards and Darnold isn’t sacked at all? Maybe, but Bradford – despite what you might read on the internet – is actually a good player. Charles Cross went out late with an ankle injury. Hopefully that heals up quickly. 
  • Fleury called a great game. Seattle was able to stick with the run game which allowed Fleury to mix it up. His playcalling on that late, game-clinching drive was clutch. That TE screen to AJ Barner was a thing of beauty. He had Darnold getting the ball out quickly which contributed to the protection. Once Fleury has his full stable of running backs, we’ll hopefully see the offense break out even more. 

The most frustrating thing about the last few weeks is that the Seahawks were clearly better than both the Niners and Denver Broncos, losing very winnable games because of turnovers and poor offensive performance. Seattle’s performance against the formerly undefeated Chiefs just underscores that point. They need to use this game as a springboard to keep playing complementary football and get this thing rolling.

Seattle is not done. The Niners lost today and sustained more injuries. This Seahawks defense will give them a chance to win every game for the rest of the season. It’s up to the offense to hold up their end of the bargain. If they play like they did today, Seattle will be right in the thick of things.

item.title: The Morning After: The Steelers’ defense has reached elite territory
item.description: The Steelers’ defense has become one of the NFL’s best.
item.content:encoded:
Entering the 2026 season, the Pittsburgh Steelers defense felt like it was facing its expiration date. Like a hair band from the ‘80s trying to remain relevant in the 2000s – either adapt or be left behind and forgotten.

Pittsburgh’s defense had become more nostalgia act than on-field production. Sure, several future Hall of Famers are on the roster, but their numbers in 2025 were rough. They finished the 2025 season 20th in defensive EPA per play and 28th in total yards allowed. The never-changing defensive philosophy was severely hindering any chance for a motley crew Steelers defense to find any level of consistent play, and made it easy for the league’s best offenses to pick them apart.

Which is why when the Steelers hired Mike McCarthy in January, many rolled their eyes at the thought of this band going on tour again. But with the hiring of Patrick Graham, Pittsburgh got with the times. The sound changed. The vocals improved. Are these music puns doing anything for you? Yeah, me either, I’m done with them. I did a lot of completely useless ‘80s music research purely for the bit. Would a Duran Duran reference to their 2004 album Astronaut save it?

You get the point. The Steelers adapted and they evolved, which is something they needed to if they wanted to make any sort of noise during the 2026 season.

Through seven weeks, the Steelers are tied for sixth in defensive EPA per play. They’re also allowing the sixth-fewest yards per game. DVOA wise, the Steelers rank seventh in the NFL, and they are second in DVOA against the run, trailing only the Jacksonville Jaguars. And while the entire season has seen the Steelers’ defensive pendulum swing to the other side, the last three games in particular have been especially terrific.

Since Week 5, the Steelers have allowed just three touchdowns, which is tied with the Minnesota Vikings for the fewest in the league over that span. Their defensive success rate ranks third in the league, and their success rate against the run is the NFL’s best over that span, nearly a full two percentage points better than the second-place Chicago Bears. Passing wise, they are giving up just 5.67 yards per attempt during this three-game win streak, and they’ve picked off three passes compared to just two touchdown passes.

This is an elite unit by just about every measure there is to offer. And if the offense can continue its own level of success (eighth in EPA per play, fourth in rush success rate since Week 5), this is a team that can hang with anyone.

It’s the morning after game day, and don’t look now, but the Steelers are good.

Big Patrick Queen game

I don’t think there is a player more scrutinized by Steelers fans than Patrick Queen, but he had one of his best games as a Steeler on Sunday. Queen led the team with 10 tackles, one of which was a sack that would end up being the final play of the game for the Saints’ offense. He was credited with three run stops and seven impact plays, per Sumer Sports, which was the second-highest of any linebacker in Week 7. Only Blake Cashman of the Minnesota Vikings had more – a really good outing from No. 6.

Jaylen Warren continues his fantastic season

I’m going to do a stand-alone piece on this because his play is more than deserving of it. So if this seems a little bare bones, don’t worry. Warren had 101 yards on the ground and added 36 yards as a receiver. The tear that he is on right now is pretty special, and I’ll have more on it later.

Quick hitters

  • The third-down defense was obviously an issue. Can’t allow a team to convert on 50 percent of their third downs.
  • After a Hall of Fame performance agains the Bucs, Jalen Ramsey had a rough outing. Per Sumer Sports, he gave up nine receptions on 10 targets for 78 yards and a touchdown.
  • Payton Wilson had a strong outing with six tackles, two run stuffs, and the interception in the red zone that completely swung the game.
  • T.J. Watt is firmly back in the elite pass rusher conversation. He had a sack – and what should have been a forced fumble and recovery that was overturned. Nevertheless, he is fourth in the NFL in sacks and fifth in pressure to sack percentage among all players who have played 100 snaps.
  • The 2-1 carry ratio for Warren and Rico Dowdle is a good one. Warren finished with 18 carries to Dowdle’s nine. Overall, Warren had 21 touches to Dowdle’s 15, with the latter adding a very solid 86 yards from scrimmage.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.title: Tom Brady's criticism of officials tests limits of what a team owner can say
item.description: Brady is prohibited from "egregious" criticism of calls.
item.content:encoded:
Tom Brady's insistence on working for Fox while owning a piece of the Raiders creates potential complications beyond the restrictions on his access to team facilities and practices. When it comes to criticizing game officials, there's a line he can't cross.

As the league has previously explained it, Brady is prohibited from being "egregiously critical of officiating" or "call[ing] into question the integrity of an official or the crew."

On Sunday in Detroit, Brady criticized multiple officiating decisions. The overriding question is whether the league office will regard the criticism as "egregious."

In the third quarter, Packers linebacker Brenton Cox Jr. knocked Lions quarterback Jared Goff to the ground after a throw. The officials called Cox for roughing the passer.

"Not much at all," Brady said over the replay. "It's coming off the block. His face is buried. I don't know about that. I mean . . . that's a tough one."

Fox rules analyst (and former NFL senior V.P. of officiating) Dean Blandino agreed. "He's coming off the block," Blandino said. "You really want to see more force there. It's almost like he's just trying to keep himself up. There's no real extension. I don't like that as roughing."

"I don't like it either," Brady said.

In the fourth quarter, after Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes was flagged for an illegal hit on Packers running back MarShawn Lloyd, Brady was blunt.

"What?" Brady said. "There's no way. . . . Oh, come on, man. Come on. [Jordan] Love throws it over the middle. There's linebackers in the middle. He's just turning his right shoulder away from it. That's allowed 99 out of 100 [times]. . . . It's a bang-bang play. I know in super slow-mo every little minute frame looks like a lot, but when you're on the field, you've got to pursue that ball. If [Lloyd] catches it, [Barnes] needs force to knock him on the ground. He needs force to knock that ball out. . . . He can't go in there and put his hand on him."

Later, during Detroit's game-winning drive, Brady sounded off on a questionable roughing the passer call, after Packers defensive tackle Karl Brooks hit Lions quarterback Jared Goff following a throw.

"Oh my goodness, what is that?" Brady said. "There's no way! Brooks on the tackle. Kind of makes a great play. It's a bang-bang play. He rolls off his body. It's a great throw by Goff. It's definitely not roughing the passer. I mean, you just — you're just ripping through the line of scrimmage to try to get the quarterback on the ground. Look, I love Goff standing there in the pocket. But you just can't keep tacking on 15 yards."

Blandino agreed with Brady's assessment again. "It wasn't late," Blandino said. "They might have said head/neck area. But this is not head/neck area. His head is up. That's teach-tape tackle. That's not roughing the passer."

Each of the calls seemed unwarranted. But the league's rules don't create an exception based on accuracy of the criticism. Team personnel (including owners) can only say so much when it comes to publicly criticizing officials.

Is it "egregious"? The folks at Merriam-Webster define the term as "very noticeable." If that's the same definition the NFL uses, Brady's comments qualify.

It has nothing to do with Brady's role as a broadcaster. (If anything, Kevin Burkhardt's criticism of the calls was even stronger.) However, the league has a policy that muzzles team personnel, including owners.

If Brady gets dinged for this, it's not because he's working for Fox. It's because he's working for Fox while owning a piece of the Raiders.

item.title: Congrats to Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie for inducting himself into team Hall of Fame
item.description: It’s nice to treat yourself.
item.content:encoded:
It’s an incredible honor when you’re inducted into an NFL team’s Hall of Fame. It’s a little weird when you’re the owner and you do it yourself. In the midst of an awful season and questions swirling about the Eagles’ future, owner Jeffrey Lurie is giving himself a nice little mid-season victory lap.

On Monday the Eagles announced that Lurie would be entering the team’s Hall of Fame, complete with an extensive quote by Lurie himself.

Lurie has been a fantastic owner since he took over the Eagles in 1994. He has done amazing work in the community and helped steward the team to two Super Bowl wins over the last decade. Still, putting yourself in the team Hall of Fame is really on the nose. There’s no doubt this was a move with an eye cast to the future. Lurie recently turned 75 — and men of a certain age get existential about how they’ll be remembered. When you’re a billionaire with the power to make things happen, you become desperate to erect monuments to yourself, leave a mark, grappling with the realization that you might be gone soon.

Does Lurie belong in the Eagles Hall of Fame? Definitely. Is he the man to enshrine himself? No. Let’s be real, nobody should go to the effort of giving themself a pat on the back. The team will eventually bounce to his kids, or be sold off — and there could easily be a succession clause that asks for him to be honored by the Eagles. It would be wholly deserved then.

Making a big statement about how honored you are to enter a Hall of Fame for a team you own — especially during a season that is going down in flames. Not exactly the best optics.

item.title: Seahawks vs. Bears odds: Seattle opens as home favorite against Chicago
item.description: The Seahawks are three-point favorites against a 5-2 Bears team on Monday Night Football.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks will host the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football in Week 8, with FanDuel Sportsbook opening Seattle as a 3-point favorite. The Seahawks are priced at -172 on the moneyline, while Chicago sits at +144. The over/under is set at 46.5 points.

Chicago enters the matchup with a 5-2 record after defeating the New England Patriots 30-24 on Thursday night, getting a mini-bye before the matchup against the Seahawks. Seattle, meanwhile, improved to 4-3 with a convincing 20-3 win over the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday Night Football. The Seahawks’ defense dominated Patrick Mahomes and company, while the offense leaned on its running game and another outstanding performance from Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

Despite Chicago’s better record, oddsmakers are giving Seattle the edge at Lumen Field. For comparison, Kansas City opened as a three-point underdog at Seattle in Week 7 despite entering that game undefeated, and Seattle won comfortably.

The total of 46.5 points suggests expectations of a more competitive scoring affair than Sunday’s defensive battle against Kansas City. Chicago scored 30 points against New England, while Seattle held the Chiefs to just a field goal, making this a compelling matchup between a productive Bears offense led by Ben Johnson, and a Seahawks defense coming off one of its strongest performances of the season.

Seattle will look to carry that momentum into another prime-time game, but Chicago presents a different challenge. The Bears will arrive in Seattle looking to prove they belong among the NFC’s contenders.

item.title: Chiefs’ offense had a historically poor showing in loss to Seahawks
item.description: Kansas City’s quarterback was unable to lift the flailing unit around him in Seattle.
item.content:encoded:
This season, the Kansas City Chiefs reinvigorated the offense around quarterback Patrick Mahomes and started generating explosive plays again, whether through handoffs to running back Kenneth Walker or downfield throws off play action.

In Week 7, the Seattle Seahawks kept the Chiefs from finding any long gains, and suddenly, the offense looked as horrendous as it has in any game in the era of quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

Mahomes finished with 165 yards on 19 of 33 passing, posting the fifth-lowest marks of his career for passing yards per attempt (5) and passer rating (58.3).

It was only the second time Kansas City has scored three or fewer points with Mahomes at quarterback. The other game was also in Week 7, in 2021, a 27-3 loss to the Tennessee Titans.

According to NFL Researcher on X, the Chiefs totaled the fewest yards and first downs of any game started by Mahomes.

It was a frustrating night for the two-time MVP, who played without two of his top wideouts — Rashee Rice (hamstring) and Tyquan Thornton (dislocated ankle) — and his starting right tackle, Jaylon Moore (concussion).

Still, Mahomes and the Chiefs’ offense have produced more in similarly tough spots before. It was a failure from start to finish in Seattle. Head coach Andy Reid pointed to one key factor in the abysmal performance after the game in his post-game press conference.

“You got to keep yourself out of third-and-long situations,” Reid said at the podium. “You’ve got to do better on first and second down. We can do better. We had some penalties in there also that got us going in the wrong direction. Got to take care of those.”

On Kansas City’s opening drive, the Chiefs moved the chains on third-and-7, but the officials called an illegal shift on tight end Travis Kelce, wiping away any offensive momentum. Late in the first half, two incompletions opened a drive, and the Chiefs failed to convert on third-and-10 with a screen pass to running back Emmett Johnson.

Those possessions put the Chiefs in a hole, and Mahomes couldn’t dig him and the unit out of it. He threw an interception on a second-down pass in Seattle territory that could’ve been avoided. He also fumbled on a third-down play when he didn’t feel the pressure, ending a promising possession.

Mahomes reflected on the game at the podium in Seattle.

“In order to have success in this league, you got to be able to sustain drives, and we weren’t able to do that,” Mahomes acknowledged. “And obviously they contained the explosive plays. So it’s stuff we have to continue to get better at. You can’t have those mistakes versus this defense.”

At one point in the first half, Mahomes was 7/14 with an interception and just 63 yards. He had five straight incompletions in the second quarter, including the interception.

“Especially early in the game, I thought my feet were kind of getting me into trouble, where I could have maybe sat in the pocket and made some of the throws down the field,” Mahomes admitted. “I got better a little bit later in the game. But at the same time, when you play a team like that, you can’t let them get ahead and get into a game they want to play.”

As the gunslinger settled into primetime, his receivers couldn’t step up with him, and the absence of Thornton was felt as heavily as it has since he was injured. When the offense found a rhythm in the second half, a drop by wide receiver Xavier Worthy had many in Chiefs Kingdom — including Mahomes — wanting to pull their hair out.

These feelings are part of a blowout loss, and the Chiefs quarterback knows it’s important to embrace them to move forward.

“The biggest thing is you got to feel it. This sucks,” Mahomes said. “You don’t want to perform like this in primetime on a big moment like this. You got to feel it on that plane ride home and understand that it sucks, but then how can you build off it?”

Whatever the solution is, it needs to happen for the offense to keep humming as it did in Weeks 1-4. Running back Kenneth Walker was held to just 36 rushing yards, which is simply not a winning formula.

“We have to help [Walker],” Mahomes said. “When they put so many eggs in that basket of stopping the run game, we have to have the play-action game and the movement game to be able to throw the ball. And if we’re not proving that, they’re going to continue to put those guys at the line of scrimmage, and that is hard for the run game.”

item.title: Eagles-Cowboys Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 7 enemy
item.description: ﻿﻿﻿﻿Opponent insight on Philadelphia’s upcoming matchup.
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Eagles are in primetime once again as they host the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on Monday night. The Birds will be looking to break a four-game losing streak to help keep their season alive.

In order to preview this Week 7 NFC East battle, I reached out to our enemies over at Blogging The Boys. The deft Dave Halprin kindly took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers.

1 – The Cowboys are 2-4 and Brian Schottenheimer seems to be in the crosshairs. To what extent deserve does he deserve blame for this team’s struggles?

He has to take a lot of the blame this year, and not just because as a head coach you have to take the blame when your team is stumbling. It’s not like he was handed a roster devoid of talent. Maybe some of it was overrated, but there are legitimate stars on the roster. Additionally, his play-calling and in-game management decisions have been puzzling at times, and that is a kind way of describing it. A lot of this concerns the offense, but he also kept a special teams coach from last year who was very poor in 2025. Most expected he would be let go in the offseason, but Schottenheimer kept him and it has definitely hurt us more than helped. 

In his own defense, during his time in Dallas Schottenheimer has been saddled by a really poor defense, something we’ll discuss a little later. But the offense seems to be regressing, that’s his side of the ball, and this is largely with the same personnel that was an elite offense in 2025. This has all been surprising as the Cowboys fanbase and punditry felt like Schotty did a fairly good job in 2025, and it seemed to be a very positive offseason. So this poor start was not what was envisioned. 

2 – Christian Parker is off to a rough start. Is there any confidence he’ll rebound? Especially now that Mike Pettine is here? Beyond coaching, how much is personnel an issue?

I think it is way too early to decide anything about Christian Parker. Unlike Schottenheimer, he was handed a defense that has had very little success recently and not much star power. He is patching things together with players who may not all fit his scheme. He has also been hit incredibly hard with injuries, especially in the secondary. So the hope is Parker is fighting some strong headwinds because the product currently on the field has been the problem for most of the season.  

The Cowboys suffer from two problems, and when you mix them together they are lethal. First is they can’t rush the passer. Second is they have trouble covering receivers. You can probably work out the problem from that. Their edge players have moments when they create pressure, but actually hitting and sacking the QB is not their specialty at the moment. It feels like they will have to blitz more to make things happen in that department. The secondary has been wiped out by injury, and they are having coverage breakdowns regularly. So blitzing that doesn’t get home leaves a vulnerable secondary even more vulnerable.

There have been moments when you can see Parker’s vision. The second half of the Packers game was one of those moments, and there have been other stretches too. I think you have to give him at least the whole season until you can really start making an informed decision about what he’s trying to do. 

3 – The Dallas defense hasn’t been good but it’s not like the offense has played well over the past two weeks, either. What’s the problem there?

There are plenty of theories about what is going wrong with the offense. The big overarching thing that is happening is that both the Bucs and the Packers decided to blitz Dallas a lot and trust their corners to cover. Previously, this was a foolish decision because Dak Prescott was statistically one of the best QBs versus the blitz. The Cowboys used to pray teams would blitz them. Suddenly, the blitz is working. Prescott has two bad games in a row. Some say it is Schottenheimer’s route concepts and play-calling. Some say the offensive line is doing a poor job of identifying the blitzers. Some say the lack of commitment to the run game is putting Prescott into too much danger. 

I would say that it is a mix of all that going on. But it is incumbent on Schottenheimer to get that fixed. He calls the plays and the offense is his specialty. 

4 – What’s the biggest matchup in the Cowboys’ favor and the biggest matchup against their favor?

Right now, the Cowboys best weapon is the combo of Dak Prescott and wide receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. On paper at least. Even that has not been smooth throughout the season and has really suffered in the last few weeks. Now, lots of fans would tell you that the Cowboys should commit more to their running game with an offensive line that is built to run in the middle. That was very effective last year, but we’ve yet to see it take hold this year.

The Cowboys biggest disadvantage is their coverage in the secondary, especially when it comes to third down. They are just terrible, teams are converting 3rd-and-longs against us at an embarrassing rate. And don’t think that young, unknown quarterbacks can’t get it done either because Jalon Daniels for the Bucs did it. 

5 – Who wins this game and why? With the Cowboys currently listed as 4.5-point road favorites, what’s your score prediction?

I’m going to say Dallas is going to win it, but with absolutely no conviction behind that. It’s more because I don’t want the season to be over this early and going to 2-5 on the year feels like the end. The slight improvement in the defense in the second half last week gives me hope that Mike Pettine is starting to help. And you guys are certainly going through your own amount of turmoil. Let’s say: Cowboys 27 – Eagles 23.

item.title: Andy Reid addresses report about kicking Chiefs player out of meeting
item.description: Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid asked Chiefs lineman Josh Simmons to leave a team meeting, per a report. Here's what Reid said when asked about the incident.
item.content:encoded:
Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid hardly addressed the NFL Network report that he and Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes asked second-year tackle Josh Simmons to leave a team meeting.

"I've said so much on him," Reid told reporters after the Chiefs fell to the Seattle Seahawks on "Sunday Night Football."

Chiefs Vice President of Medicine and Performance Rick Burkholder spoke to the media Oct. 22, and Reid referred to Burkholder's comments, in which he provided a timeline for the bulging, herniated disc that has kept Simmons off the field. The team placed Simmons, the 32nd overall pick in the 2025 draft, on injured reserve again and he will not return until Nov. 22 against the Arizona Cardinals at the earliest.

"Rick's talked about him, this and that. Things happen. That's no reason he's been put on IR," Reid said when asked directly about the report that said Simmons was asked to leave a meeting.

"He's got a bad back," Reid said. "He's got to get that worked out. But that's the main thing. I'll leave it at that."

NFL Network reported Simmons, who returned to practice Wednesday, Oct. 14, was sitting with his feet up during an offensive team meeting. Reid asked him to put his feet down, per the report, and Simmons replied that he had to sit in that manner because of back discomfort. Reid then told Simmons to seek treatment if he was in pain, according to witnesses cited in the NFL Network report, and when Simmons protested more, Mahomes also spoke up.

Burkholder previously told reporters that Simmons attempted to rehab the disk issue in his lumbar spine – which caused the calf discomfort he felt during camp – before a lack of progress encouraged the medical team to shut him down again.

item.title: Fantasy Football Stock Report: Chase Brown continues to struggle while 3 other RB2s thrive in Week 7
item.description: Matt Okada highlights the biggest risers and fallers for fantasy football going into Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
As I write this on Sunday night, 13 of 14 Week 7 games are in the books (with Monday night remaining) and the fantasy season is now nearing the halfway point. Still, things are changing every week. Promising improvements. Concerning trends. Performances that change our early outlook on players and teams. As always, some of these shifting perspectives will have permanent ramifications in fantasy.

With that in mind, I've compiled another full fantasy stock report. These are the most notable risers and fallers heading into Week 8. 

STOCK UP

Zay Flowers, WR, Ravens

Here are the wide receivers I'd rather have rest-of-season than Zay Flowers: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, CeeDee Lamb and Amon-Ra St. Brown. And Malik Nabers is a toss-up. That's it. The Ravens' No. 1 WR just snagged eight of 11 targets for 137 yards and a touchdown from Tyler Huntley. He's second in the league in yards per route run, behind Smith-Njigba, and third in the league in fantasy points per route run, behind JSN and Mike Evans (shoutout Evans, by the way). And I don't even think it's debatable anymore that he's the best YAC threat at the position right now. He would very likely be the WR2 overall if not for his early injury and a couple middling games with Huntley at the helm. With Lamar Jackson close to a return and Flowers healthy — and a few brilliant matchups on the horizon — he's set for an elite second half of the fantasy season.

Bucky Irving, RB, Buccaneers

It's been a feast-or-famine stretch for Bucky Irving lately, but Sunday brought a 23.5-point feast on 24 carries for 106 yards and two touchdowns. Prior to Week 7, Irving had scored fewer than seven fantasy points in three of four games ... and 30.5 in the fourth (against Dallas). But there are reasons to believe this wasn't just another flukey peak en route to several more valleys.

For one, Baker Mayfield was back for this game (with a glove on his throwing hand). While he did next to nothing — because he didn't have to — it likely matters to defensive game plans and to the workload for Irving. For another, while the fantasy output has been spotty, Irving has seen at least 15 carries in six straight games. The only backs with more 15-carry games this year are Jonathan Taylor and Derrick Henry. It would be nice if Irving were more involved as a receiver, which would raise the floor just a bit, but in what feels like a very shallow RB market this season, Irving is a worthy RB2.

Quinshon Judkins, RB, Browns

In his return from a one-week absence due to an ankle injury, Quinshon Judkins had his best fantasy day of the season by far. He took 17 carries for 96 yards and two touchdowns, after scoring just once all season entering Sunday. And, while the Titans defense can be blamed for some of Judkins' efficiency, he also looked excellent ... for perhaps the first time this year. Like Irving, he's had a very high volume floor — 14+ touches in every single game — but has been mostly middling for fantasy.

It's worth noting that Dylan Sampson returned to action in this game and had 77 yards on nine touches of his own. But it's also worth noting that the Browns are 5-2 and have won five of their last six, and that the "toughest" remaining opponent on their schedule, at least by current record, is the 5-2 Steelers ... who Judkins tagged for 18.6 fantasy points in Week 4. The concept that Judkins can't thrive because Browns' game scripts are so unfavorable doesn't hold much water right now, and after Pittsburgh he gets the Saints (the best RB matchup in fantasy). He's a low-end RB2 and those are hard to come by these days.

Cam Skattebo, RB, Giants

This is probably the easiest "Stock Up" of the entire season. A week after he was relegated to six snaps and zero touches in a clearly punitive benching for fumble issues, Cam Skattebo returned with a vengeance in Week 7. Not only was he the runaway RB1 with 17 carries (to Tyrone Tracy Jr.'s six and Devin Singletary's five), but he racked up a career-best 124 yards on those carries, including a strong 16-yard touchdown and 42-yarder to set up the game-winner in overtime against Houston. He held on to the ball and went "full Skattebo" several times throughout the game, finishing with a season-high 18.6 fantasy points.

More than anything, it was incredibly clear that John Harbaugh wants Skattebo as his RB1 and that the Week 7 message was clearly received. Skattebo did reportedly tweak his hamstring at the end of the game, but New York has a Week 8 bye, so he has time to rest up. Looking ahead, he fits right into the same tier as Irving and Judkins: high-volume running backs on somewhat questionable offenses who should slot into low-end RB2 range down the stretch.

Omar Cooper Jr., WR, Jets

While I'm hesitant to buy all the way in on Jets rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. following two big games, he is flashing explosive upside that you don't find lying around in fantasy. After catching one 30-yard pass in the season opener and then missing four games on injured reserve, Cooper has had 100+ yards and a touchdown in consecutive weeks. He caught a 48-yarder in Week 6 against the Patriots and then a 52-yarder and a 60-yarder in Week 7.

Importantly, he's also caught 11 total passes on 12 targets these past two games ... while Garrett Wilson has just six catches on nine targets. I wouldn't say Wilson has been replaced as the WR1, but it is notable that when he draws a defense's toughest matchups or a double-team, Cooper is freed up to thrive against lesser coverage. We'll want to see the shifting target share hold for another couple weeks before drawing any aggressive conclusions, but Cooper is absolutely worth adding on waivers — if he's still available — or you can try to acquire him before the price gets too high.

STOCK DOWN

Garrett Wilson, WR, Jets

We'll start the Stock Down section where we ended the Stock Up. But it's not just Cooper's rise that's hurting Wilson's fantasy value. He had three catches on four targets for 27 yards back in Week 4 against the Bears (with Cooper on IR) and has now logged fewer than seven fantasy points in three of his last four games. And, frankly, this is kind of what Wilson does. He's typically a target monster in New York, but he also tends to underperform, for one reason or another, in far more games than we'd like from a WR1. He's now just the WR24 in points per game on the year and the WR42 over the last month.

As I said with Cooper above, I don't think the roles have reversed in New York, and I expect Wilson to continue putting up strong performances on a near-weekly basis. However, with Cooper breaking out, Wilson's greatest strength — an elite target share — could suffer a hit down the stretch. He's definitely more of a low-end WR2 in my book and I wouldn't mind shopping him for a more consistent producer with a lesser name (or for Zay Flowers).

Chase Brown, RB, Bengals

It's starting to get really ugly for Chase Brown in Cincinnati and in fantasy. He has not topped 39 rushing yards in any of the last three games and has single-digit fantasy totals in four of his last five. The only reason it's not five straight is that he caught 11 passes for 71 yards in an absurd Week 4, but that should not be expected or projected (he's averaged 3.4 catches for 14.4 yards in his other five games). He outproduced Samaje Perine on Sunday, but Perine still managed to vulture a goal-line rushing touchdown. And Joe Burrow carried the offense otherwise, with 292 passing yards and four touchdowns through the air.

Brown is just the RB25 on the season in points per game ... and his best performance was way back in Week 1, when he scored his only touchdown of the year (and just 16.3 points). Since Week 2, he's been outscored by Brian Robinson Jr., Alvin Kamara and Emanuel Wilson, among many others. That's simply not going to cut it for a back drafted to be a fringe RB1. Unless Brown pulls off a major turnaround — as he did down the stretch just last season — he is trending quickly towards bust territory.

Aaron Jones Sr., RB, Vikings

Well, it was a nice run for Aaron Jones Sr. as the solo back in Minnesota. With Jordan Mason on injured reserve from Weeks 2-5 (and a Week 6 bye), Jones averaged a monster 24.3 touches for 110.5 yards per game and was the RB13 in fantasy points per game. In Mason's return on Sunday ... Jones touched the ball nine times and totaled 26 yards. Mason, on the other hand, racked up 15 totes for 68 yards, while playing 62.5% of the snaps (to just 26.8% for Jones).

The only glimmer of hope here might be that the Vikings are about to enter a much tougher stretch of opponents and are very unlikely to continue their unbeaten streak, or at least to do so without struggle. That could mean that game scripts favor Jones (the more active receiver) over Mason for the foreseeable future ... but even if they do, Jones will be an inconsistent half of a committee backfield. It's probably too late to trade him for a decent return, but you simply cannot expect Jones to maintain RB2 fantasy value moving forward.

Isaiah Likely, TE, Giants

The optimistic outlook for Isaiah Likely's Week 7 dud is that the Texans defense found a way to stifle him — which they had done to tight ends all season — and that his disappearance had nothing to do with the J.J. McCarthy takeover at quarterback. Considering Likely caught two of three targets for 44 yards and a touchdown in McCarthy's one quarter two weeks ago, it's not blind optimism ... but there's still reason for concern.

Likely caught just two passes on four targets (for 12 yards) on Sunday, after seeing 11+ targets in each of the three games prior and 9.8 targets per game over the first six weeks. He had been making a case as a top-five tight end, only clearly behind Trey McBride and Brock Bowers, but that case gets a little tougher after 2.2 fantasy points. Heading into a Week 8 bye, Likely, McCarthy and the entire offense will have some time to gel a little further, and I expect things to bounce back a bit on the other side. But it's also possible we just get intermittent disappearances from Likely — he also scored just 2.3 points in Week 3 — as he is not quite the dominant force that McBride or Bowers are.

item.title: Patriots release punter Bryce Baringer
item.description: The Patriots are parting ways with their punter of the last three seasons.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots are officially making a change at the punter position.

Bryce Baringer, who had played the role since his arrival in 2023 but most recently found himself on injured reserve, is being released by the team. NFL insider Jordan Schultz was first to report the move.

Baringer, 27, originally joined the Patriots as a sixth-round selection in the 2023 draft. The Michigan State product went on to appear in all 55 possible regular season and playoff games over his first three years with the club, serving a dual role as punter as well as holder on field goal and extra point tries.

In total, Baringer punted the ball 247 times for an average of 47.1 yards per kick. Subtracting opponents’ returns, his net punting average stands at 40.6 yards a punt.

Baringer entered the 2026 season as the featured option at the position, but he suffered an undisclosed injury in the second preseason game. The move eventually prompted the Patriots to sign veteran free agent Mitch Wishnowsky and place the incumbent on injured reserve. Now healthy again, Baringer will not be activated to the active roster but instead let go by the team.

Wishnowsky has played all seven of New England’s games so far this season. He has punted 22 times for an average of 47.1 yards with a net of 41.2.

The 4-3 Patriots will travel to Miami this week to take on the 1-5 Dolphins.
