item.title: Jaguars 2026 Rookie Analysis So Far
item.description: Was the criticism of Jacksonville’s 2026 draft class overblown? The early returns are making Gladstone’s case for him.
item.content:encoded:
Back in April, James Gladstone went against the consensus on all but one pick, and the consensus on Gladstone was that he’d pay for it. Some had him pegged as the worst GM in the game before any of his picks had taken a snap. Six games in, that verdict is already falling apart. Not every selection has made an impact yet, but the early returns have been hard to argue with.

Early hits

Nate Boerkircher

Nobody took more heat on draft night than Boerkircher, a largely unknown tight end Draft Twitter couldn’t wait to pile on. His box score is modest: six catches for 52 yards, and a one-handed touchdown grab last week that almost validated the pick on its own. But the numbers don’t capture what a key piece he’s been to the offensive success. Boerkircher has become the dirty-work blocker in heavier personnel packages the team desperately missed last season, and the Jaguars now lead the NFL in EPA per play (0.205) in multi-TE sets, with him playing a big role.

Emmanuel Pregnon

Pregnon was the one pick that lined up with the consensus board, and he’s delivered. He won the left guard job in camp and has started every game, with the ups and downs you’d expect, but he’s been about as good as you could hope for from a third-round rookie guard. The one thing to clean up is the penalties: six, tied for the league lead. That said, Pregnon looks like an absolute steal for the Jaguars and the needle is only pointing up for his potential.

Josh Cameron

Josh Cameron might be the best argument against the doubters. A polarizing wide receiver prospect in the draft community, he lasted until the sixth round and has delivered: eight catches for 117 yards, with sure hands and a willingness to block. He’s been impressive enough that he’s getting snaps over Brian Thomas Jr. He’s an even bigger weapon on special teams, averaging 27.2 yards on nine kick returns (245 yards, long of 46), and he’d have had a return touchdown if not for a questionable holding call. He’s added five special teams tackles on top of it.

Opportunities coming

Albert Regis

Regis was drafted as a run stuffer out of Texas A&M, which fits this Jacksonville defense perfectly, but he also flashed as a pass rusher in the preseason. He has played in just three games and logged 22 defensive snaps so far after missing the earlier part of the season with an injury, but that added versatility makes it easy to see his role growing as the season goes on.

Tanner Koziol

Koziol was drafted as essentially a big slot, and he wasn’t considered much of a blocker coming out of Houston. That said, blocking is almost all he’s done so far, and he’s done a solid job of it. He has appeared in four games, logging 30 offensive snaps, mostly in the heavy tight end packages that have the Jaguars leading the league in EPA per play, plus 15 special teams snaps. He hasn’t caught a pass yet, but he was a real receiving weapon for the Cougars, and it will be fun to see him get a chance to make a play on offense.

Gaps in the process

Jalen Huskey

Huskey was a third-round pick at No. 100, drafted as an experienced defender who knows how to play the game and brings versatility in the secondary. That kind of profile is supposed to translate quickly, which makes the lack of playing time tough to explain. He has been active for just one game, where he played two special teams snaps, and he hasn’t seen a defensive snap. A pick that high should be pushing for playing time by now, particularly with the injuries at safety, but that hasn’t happened.

Wesley Williams

Williams was picked just 19 picks later, and he came at edge rusher, one of the Jaguars’ biggest areas of need. He was drafted as an experienced pass rusher who consistently gets pressure, a high-floor, low-ceiling depth piece. That’s what makes it a tougher look: a player whose selling point is that he’s ready now has been a healthy scratch all season. It’s one of the few real knocks on Gladstone’s board so far.

TBD

CJ Williams

Nobody expected much from a sixth-round receiver, so 10 offensive snaps and 6 on special teams aren’t a concern. He made countless plays in training camp, though, which gives him a case for a bigger role if injuries hit the receiver room.

Zach Durfee

The seventh-round edge rusher out of Washington has been on injured reserve all season, though the injury hasn’t been specified. He’s expected back this year, so he could still provide some pass-rush depth in the second half.

Parker Hughes

Hughes was drafted with special teams in mind, an athletic linebacker and a sure tackler. He’s been on injured reserve all season, with the injury also unspecified, so that role is still waiting for him.

Early verdict

Six games is a small sample, but the early evidence points one way: the people who wrote this class off before it played a snap were wrong about more than they were right. Boerkircher and Cameron are already making real contributions, Pregnon has held down the left side of the line, and Regis and Koziol look like they’re on their way to bigger roles. The one legitimate knock is Huskey and Wesley Williams, two high picks who haven’t earned playing time yet. The second half will tell us whether that’s a blip or a flaw in the process.

Early grade: B

What would you grade this draft class through six weeks, Jags fans?

item.title: Zaire Franklin dealing with hairline fracture, Sean Rhyan believed to have high-ankle sprain
item.description: The Packers have a couple of impact players who are dealing with injuries.
item.content:encoded:
The Packers have a couple of impact players who are dealing with injuries.

According to Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, linebacker Zaire Franklin is dealing with a hairline fracture in his leg, while center Sean Rhyan is believed to have suffered a high-ankle sprain.

Franklin's injury occurred in practice last week. He missed Sunday's game against the Lions but is expected to return without missing much more time. The team did not place him on injured reserve, which is another indication of his status.

Rhyan went down during the first half of Sunday's loss to Detroit. If his high-ankle sprain diagnosis is confirmed, he's likely to be out for four-to-six weeks.

Green Bay has a short week coming up, as they will host the Panthers on Thursday night.

item.title: Landon Dickerson teases return ahead of Eagles-Cowboys game
item.description: Philadelphia’s Pro Bowl guard is expected to be back in the starting lineup.
item.content:encoded:
It looks like Landon Dickerson is returning to the starting lineup for the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 7 game against the Dallas Cowboys.

The three-time Pro Bowl guard shared a picture of himself running out of the Lincoln Financial Field tunnel with the caption “Let’s go! 🦅” to his verified Instagram page on Sunday night:

This developments tracks with what we’ve seen over the past week. Dickerson was taking first-team left guard reps during media-attended portions of practice last week. After previously being limited in practice, he was upgraded to full participation prior to being ruled questionable to play on Saturday’s final injury report.

Dickerson is set to suit up for the first time since Week 1, when he mightily struggled against the Washington Commanders. Dickerson admitted he was a “complete liability” in that game. We’ll soon see if the time off actually helped him get healthier of if he’ll continue to struggle.

If he’s actually healthy, Dickerson’s return could provide the Eagles’ running game with a much-needed boost. He’ll be an upgrade on Willie Lampkin, who has provided admirable effort but isn’t an ideal starting guard. But, again, it remains to be seen if Dickerson will actually play well.

The Eagles have until 4:00 PM Eastern on Monday to officially activate Dickerson from injured reserve. They currently have three open roster spots.

Speaking of, it sounds like the Eagles could look to activate rookie tight end Eli Stowers from injured reserve. Expectations for him should be kept in check considering his offseason struggles.

item.title: Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 8: Caleb Douglas breaks out, Omar Cooper Jr. stays hot
item.description: Omar Cooper Jr. stayed hot with another 100 yards and a touchdown in Week 7. Fellow rookie Caleb Douglas also broke out with two touchdowns of his own. Both players headline the list of best waiver wire targets for Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
With one game left in Week 7, it's time to hit the waiver wire. These are my biggest waiver wire and FAAB targets for Week 8. Every player in this article is available in at least half of all Yahoo leagues.

Week 7 Stock Up, Stock Down: Jordan Mason’s runway has cleared
Rivers McCown highlights four fantasy players whose fantasy football stock rose in Week 7 of the NFL season and four whose stock fell.
  • Rivers McCown,

▶ Quarterback

Jacoby Brissett, Cardinals

Brissett isn't the free square QB1 he was in 2025, but that should change for at least one week when he takes on the Cowboys on Sunday. Pending their Monday Night Football game, the Cowboys are allowing the fifth-most fantasy points to opposing quarterbacks. They rank dead last in EPA per dropback allowed. This is the easiest matchup in the league.

Michael Penix, Falcons

After his second 20-point fantasy outing in a row, Penix is up to ninth in the league in EPA per dropback. He’s top-five in both touchdown rate (6.3 percent) and yards per attempt (8.0). Penix gets a tough matchup with the Bucs this week, so he isn’t a premier Week 8 streamer, but he is still the best talent-based bet on waivers right now.

Malik Willis, Dolphins

Like Penix, Willis is starting to heat up with his first and second 20-point fantasy outings of the year coming in his past two games. Week 7 was his best day as a passer by far. His 66.7 percent completion rate and 9.9 yards per attempt both go down as season highs. He also found the end zone on the ground for the second week in a row. Willis is only a QB2 for Week 8, but that’s as good as it gets on the waiver wire.

J.J. McCarthy, Giants

The Giants have Week 8 off, so McCarthy is only a long-term play, but he might be the best season-long bet Superflex players get to make this year. McCarthy has been lights out through five quarters with the Giants. Among quarterbacks with at least 50 dropbacks, NINE is 11th in EPA per play and fifth in completion percent over expected. He’s averaging over 10 yards per pass attempt this year and will face a struggling Philly defense coming out of the bye.

J.J. McCarthy finds Nabers downfield!

NYGvsHOU on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/VZ5HPcZ4JI

— NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026

▶ Running Back

Jonah Coleman, Broncos

Coleman was activated from injured reserve over the weekend and immediately took control of the Denver backfield. His nine carries led the team and 54 rushing yards would have also led the way had Bo Nix not broken off a 62-yard rushing touchdown of his own. Coleman also led the Broncos backs in snap share (50 percent) and route rate (34 percent). It was ultimately a messy committee in Week 7, but a committee that Coleman stood atop after missing a month of football. We should expect the rookie’s role to grow in the coming weeks, even if J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey will both see touches as long as they’re healthy. I’m spending 15-20 percent of my FAAB on Coleman.

Dylan Sampson, Browns

Sampson returned to the lineup in Week 7 after missing over a month while on IR. As expected, he operated as the team’s primary back on passing downs, running a route on 42 percent of Deshaun Watson’s dropbacks. He was targeted on 19 percent of his routes, resulting in three grabs for 32 yards to go along with his 45 rushing yards on six carries. Without many carries or goal line work to his name, Sampson is only worth a look in PPR leagues. As long as you get the full point per catch, he’ll be an RB3 going forward.

Bam Knight, Cardinals

Knight played a 1B role in Week 6. While Tyler Allgeier still out-carried him (by one attempt) this week, Knight flipped him in several other usage metrics. Knight led the team with a 53 percent snap share and a 48 percent route rate. He also earned a 10 percent target share compared to seven percent for Allgeier. The backs split Arizona’s two goal line carries, though Knight added an uncaught end zone target to his expected fantasy points ledger. If Jeremiyah Love remains out this week, Knight will be a solid RB3 bet.

Chris Rodriguez, Jaguars

Rodriguez forced a backfield-by-committee before the Jags’ bye week, seeing 11 carries to Bhayshul Tuten’s 12 in Week 6. He was only targeted once but did handle the team’s only goal line carry. Favored by over a touchdown at home versus the Colts, both Tuten and C-Rod should get rolling downhill this week. The Jags then get the Titans twice over the next month, so there could be several spots where Rodriguez is a viable RB3 during November.

Kaelon Black, 49ers

Christian McCaffrey got banged up in Week 7 and missed several drives, though he did return to the game after halftime. With the backfield wide open for a few minutes, Black racked up a dozen carries for 63 yards and a score. Black is arguably the best contingent bet on the board. If anything happens to McCaffrey, he’s a plug-and-play RB1. The CMC injury might also force the 49ers to get Black more involved on a weekly basis. Unfortunately for fantasy managers, the 9ers get their bye this week, so Black won’t even be a FLEX consideration until Week 9.

Devin Singletary, Giants

Tyrone Tracy left Week 7 with a hamstring injury and did not return. Cam Skattebo then injured his hamstring on his final run of the day, a 42-yard sprint that saw him go down untouched because of the injury.

SKATTEBO BREAKS FREE FOR 42 YARDS

NYGvsHOU on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/CqU4A2DpOE

— NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026

Skattebo didn’t seem too worried about the injury after the game, telling reporters it’s a “Good thing we have a bye week.” If and Tracy can’t get healthy through the bye, Singletary would be the lead back on an offense now showing signs of life under McCarthy. Because we won’t know if Singletary has any fantasy value for over a week, this is another deep-league-only stash.

▶ Wide Receiver

Omar Cooper Jr., Jets

Cooper Jr. is somehow not rostered in half of Yahoo leagues yet. He broke out in Week 6 with a 6/103/1 receiving line and gave fantasy managers an encore on Sunday with 115 yards and a touchdown on five catches. In his two healthy games, Cooper Jr. leads the Jets with a 22 percent target share and 35 percent of their air yards. He’s averaging 4.77 yards per route run, which leads all wideouts with at least 50 routes. Zay Flowers is No. 2 on the list at 3.73. Garrett Wilson and Adonai Mitchell combined for two catches on six targets last week. Once one or both of them get going, Cooper Jr.’s numbers will take a hit. The good news is that he can afford to lose some production and still be a weekly WR3. If he’s just the alpha now, the sky is the limit for Cooper. This is a FAAB Brink’s truck situation. Spend it all.

Caleb Douglas, Dolphins

Douglas was back this week after missing a month due to an ankle injury. He ran over 80 percent of the routes, which he’s done in all three of his appearances this year, and exploded for 21 fantasy points off the back of 70 yards and two scores.

Caleb Douglas took this one all the way.

MIAvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/hb8mEQrB80

— NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026

Douglas only caught two passes on three targets, but we should expect his role to grow as he gets more practice reps under his belt. Douglas was already looking like the Dolphins’ WR1 to start the year before getting injured. He accounted for 37 percent of Malik Willis’ first-read targets in his first two games. This is another strong waiver/FAAB option. I’m getting down 20-25% of my FAAB to land Douglas.

Ja’Kobi Lane, Ravens

Lane got back on the field in Week 6 after missing a month with a fractured wrist. He only ran 58 percent of the routes but did manage five targets. He upped his route rate to 75 percent on Sunday and his target total held steady at five. Lane ran more routes and earned more opportunities than Rashod Bateman. It was his third NFL game. We’re witnessing a changing of the guard in Baltimore. If Lane can put some distance between himself and Bateman while presumably getting Lamar Jackson back next week, he should be in line for a breakout performance.

Kendrick Bourne, Cardinals

Bourne isn’t doing much with his newfound No. 2 gig in Arizona, but the role is his. He has a 66 percent route rate and a 17 percent target share in three games sans Marvin Harrison Jr. Bourne would normally be more of a WR5, but a date with the Cowboys will get him in the WR4 mix this week.

Travis Hunter, Jaguars

Hunter finally operated as a two-way player in Week 6, catching four passes for 59 yards and a score while also bringing down C.J. Stroud’s first interception of the year. The bad news is that he was only on the field for seven routes. Hunter is a fun stash if you’ve got a roster spot to burn, but it’s possible you wind up sending him back to waivers next week.

Jordyn Tyson, Saints

Tyson is available in just over half of Yahoo leagues, but that number should soar in about nine days. The Saints are on bye this week and then return to the states to face the Browns. Tyson has missed the first two months of the year with a hamstring injury, but his recovery timeline always had Week 9 as the most obvious return date. Tyson was an elite producer in college and the Saints spent the No. 8 overall pick on him. Fantasy managers should be finding any way to clear a roster spot for him if he's still on waivers.

▶ Tight End

Mason Taylor, Jets

Taylor has run at least 60 percent of the Jets’ routes in all four of his healthy games this year. He is being targeted on a respectable 17 percent of his routes, and that number has ballooned to over 25 percent in each of his past two appearances. Taylor finally cashed in on Sunday with a pair of touchdowns, plus a two-point conversion. He accounted for 23 percent of Geno Smith’s targets and 53 percent of his air yards. This role is too good to be true, but it’s clear Taylor is the starting tight end for the Jets, and a solid one at that. He’s in the TE2 mix for Week 8.

Brenton Strange, Jaguars

Strange dipped below a 50 percent roster rate over the Jags’ Week 7 bye. He was looking like a weekly TE1 going into the break. In his previous three games, Strange averaged 6.3 catches for 69 yards on 7.7 targets. He finished as a top-10 fantasy tight end in two of those three games.

Greg Dulcich, Dolphins

After a slow start to the year, Dulcich is starting to develop a modest PPR floor. He has at least four catches in three of his past four games. He was, however, held without a catch in the fourth. Dulcich led the Dolphins with a 24 percent target share in Week 7. He also tallied a 21 percent target share in Week 5, before the team’s bye. Miami’s run-first approach will prevent him from ever projecting for TE1 numbers, but you could do worse on waivers this week.

Davis Allen, Rams

I don’t buy that Allen’s two-touchdown performance in Week 7 is indicative of future fantasy points, but I’m obligated to mention the TE4 of the week in this article. Allen only ran 38 percent of the Rams’ routes, but he was targeted on 42 percent of them, allowing him to amass five targets in total. He caught four passes for 20 yards and the pair of touchdowns. As the third tight end on the team by routes, it’s hard to view Allen as anything more than a TE2 for Week 8.

item.title: E.J. Jenkins reportedly not returning to the Eagles
item.description: Former Eagles tight end finds a new NFL home.
item.content:encoded:
E.J. Jenkins is not returning to the Philadelphia Eagles after being waived by the team last week.

Jenkins is instead signing with the Atlanta Falcons’ practice squad, according to a report from Andrew DiCecco.

It’s currently unclear if the Eagles had interest in signing Jenkins to their practice squad. There was thought they might since they’d have the flexibility to temporarily elevate him to the game day roster up to three times. And they previously liked Jenkins enough to have him as their third tight end on the roster.

In any case, Jenkins joins a large number of other former Eagles players (Andy Dalton, Za’Darius Smith, Olamide Zaccheaus, Jahan Dotson, Sydney Brown, Nick Muse, Robert Longerbeam, Trey Sermon, and Cameron Williams) in Atlanta. The Falcons notably employ former Eagles executive Ian Cunningham as their general manager.

The Eagles currently have two tight ends on their active roster: Dallas Goedert and Johnny Mundt. They also have Eli Stowers and Grant Calcaterra, who are in their 21-day practice windows to be activated from injured reserve. And then there’s Zach Ertz on the practice squad.

The Eagles will likely make some more roster moves ahead of Monday’s 4:00 PM Eastern deadline to have more than just two tight ends available for their Week 7 game against the Dallas Cowboys.

item.title: Cowboys at Eagles Monday Night Football betting odds, picks and predictions: Best bets, player props
item.description: Our NFL handicapper break downs his favorite bets in the Cowboys-Eagles Monday Night Football matchup.
item.content:encoded:
It's the circle of life in the NFL, I guess. 

For the second time this season, what should have been a very compelling Monday Night Football matchup is compromised by quarterback health. 

The first time, the Eagles were headed out on the road to take on the Bears without Caleb Williams, but four weeks later, it's Philadelphia that's missing its QB1, as Jalen Hurts is reportedly out of the season with issues stemming from blood clots. 

Like the Eagles in Week 3, the Cowboys are expected to win on the road, but with a line well under a touchdown again, the betting market isn't so sure. Especially after the home 'dog scored an upset the first time around.

Dallas Cowboys (-4.5, 44.5) at Philadelphia Eagles

The Cowboys' offense is overrated. 

After a respectable start, when adjusting for garbage time and high-leverage plays like turnovers and fourth downs, the Cowboys have been tumbling down the rankings of advanced metrics like weighted EPA/Play and Success Rate. 

It hasn't helped that they've faced top-five units in the Buccaneers and Packers, but their early season numbers were propped up by facing teams outside of the top 10. Plus, if you apply time for teams' scouting what Dallas wants to do, you can see why the Cowboys can't just rely on "out-talenting" the opponent. 

Few defensive coordinators are more familiar with Dallas than Vic Fangio, and the Eagles have been better at limiting opponents' EPA/Play (a metric that's augmented by the explosiveness that the Cowboys live and die by) than they have with raw Success Rate.

It was a one-game sample size, but Tanner McKee's first start of the season in relief of Hurts went about as you might expect, as the Eagles were 26th (of 28) in the metrics above. On a positive note, McKee didn't turn the ball over, despite 45 pass attempts against the Panthers. 

DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks have already been ruled out for Monday, which won't help Philadelphia's potential for chunk yardage. However, the possible return of Saquon Barkley alters what might be asked of McKee, and makes it only more likely that the Eagles will be able to sustain long, clock-chewing drives between the 20s, against a Cowboys defense that's been known to give them up. 

With neither team compelled to put the football at risk, and the familiarity with what to expect from the opposing offense, we should expect a similar game to when the Eagles were on the other side of this scenario — a score with a combined total in mid-to-high 30s like that night in Chicago.

Bet: Under 44.5 total points (-118)

Bet the under in Cowboys-Eagles at sportsbooks right now

Player props

Dak Prescott under 9.5 rush yards (-106, DraftKings)

Nothing provides the feeling of fresh legs and a new season than September football, so we shouldn't be surprised that Dak Prescott was a little more spry in the season's first three games, running 10 times for 59 yards. 

Since then, for Prescott, it's been mostly about "chuck and duck" rather than scramble, with just four rushing attempts for 7, 6, 0, and -1 yards over the last three games. 

Against a pass defense with just a 45% pass-rush win rate, Prescott should have enough time to get the ball out — something he's realized is a better option than taking off on a cold night in Philly.

George Pickens under 4.5 receptions (+116, FanDuel)

Last season, Pickens averaged exactly one more reception and over 20 yards more per game at home, clearly enjoying the friendly confines of "Jerry World."

This season, it's even more drastic: 

  • Home: 15 receptions in two games

  • Road: 11 receptions in three games

That last number is only that high because the Cowboys found themselves in such an aggressive trailing game-state in Green Bay last Sunday night. As the favorites in this one, there shouldn't be any need to force-feed Pickens anything like the 11 targets that were sent his way to crawl over this total a week ago. 

Saquon Barkley over 13.5 receiving yards (-110, DraftKings)

On Sunday, the 49ers — devoid of quality receiving options — plotted all week to put Christian McCaffrey in the slot, and shift far enough outside the backfield to be used as a primary pass-catching option (at least, until he got hurt doing it). 

The Eagles aren't sharp enough to put that kind of plan in place on short notice, but it's the general idea that throwing to Barkley will be another way to get their best player in space. That will provide an easy outlet for McKee, while taking heat of their makeshift offensive line — a unit that's struggled to create holes for any runners. 

Anytime TD scorers

Ryan Flournoy (+370, DraftKings)

In a game we anticipate to be low-scoring, playing the Cowboys' highly-publicized weapons doesn't present much value. 

When it comes to "names," you could start including Flournoy's with Pickens and CeeDee Lamb, based on the fact he was just one snap short of those other two last week, and regularly plays over three-quarters of the time. 

Against the Eagles, whose secondary drops off in quality the deeper you go, if Prescott looks away from whoever's being covered by Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean, Flournoy might make it back-to-back games with a touchdown, and six of the last 15 going back to last season (implied odds of +150). 

Brevyn Spann-Ford (+700, DraftKings)

Another reason to like Flournoy is because of the drop in opportunity for Jake Ferguson. After a rough Week 5, he went from someone who often plays 70% of snaps to barely half in Green Bay.

Ferguson's tight end replacement for those handful of snaps was Brevyn Spann-Ford, who went from three catches on six targets in the first five games, to hauling in four of his five looks from Prescott. 

In his third year, BSF is a big, sizable, freak of an athlete at 6-foot-6 — the perfect red-zone target against the Eagles, against whom he scored his lone career touchdown last season. 

Dallas Goedert (+190, DraftKings)

The young, inexperienced quarterback's best friend is always the tight end. Sure enough, Dallas Goedert was on the other end of eight Tanner McKee targets, for six receptions, last week against the Panthers. 

That was second on the Eagles to Smith, who caught seven of 14 targets, and the lone passing touchdown. With Smith out, Goedert should slide into an even more featured role for McKee, particularly in play-action near the goal line with Barkley selling the run.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Vikings' pass rate under Kyler Murray and more key stats that may go overlooked from Week 7
item.description: Joel Smyth takes you through key stats from Week 7 and how it can help you with fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
In fantasy football, you have to look back to move forward. Fantasy points are the goal, but how a player gets there is the key. Analyst Joel Smyth breaks down 8 numbers to know from Week 7 in order to win your matchup in Week 8 and beyond.

79%

Of the RB touches between Chase Brown and Samaje Perine went to Brown. It was another tough fantasy day for Brown, but at least it was a tough day as the bellcow, rather than the split we saw in Week 5. The low point of Brown's fantasy day came when Perine got the carry from the one-yard line, one of his four touches on the day. Brown did have the other two snaps inside the five, and two carries inside the 10, but stayed at one touchdown on the season after scoring 15 in Burrow's prior 15 full games.

Brown had 11 carries, five targets and 75% of the snaps, as Perine had virtually nothing before vulturing the goal-line attempt. I would expect Brown to have games similar to Week 7, yet still maintain a workhorse role as the Bengals starter. It doesn't look like we'll see the consistent RB1 we saw last year, but better days that mirror Week 1 and 4 are coming.​

52.6%

Pass rate for the Minnesota Vikings with Kyler Murray. In the past, Vikings offenses that were not the 2025 disaster (2022-2024) dropped back to pass over 61% of the time, a top-three rate in the NFL. It's a new offense in 2026, centered around the run game and leaning on their dominant defense. The Vikings have had top defenses before and still remained pass heavy, but Kevin O'Connell has taken a turn this season, dropping well below 2025's rate. The combination of Murray being much less successful than Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold from past seasons, averaging only 6.6 yards per dropback, and the pass rate, may cause some trouble.

Jordan Addison has largely been unusable when Justin Jefferson is available, and Jefferson has been slightly below expectation in his two full games with Murray. Week 6 was a positive for Jefferson overall, but Week 7 made it back-to-back weeks with only seven targets. The 11.1 half-PPR PPG in those two games is a letdown considering the easy matchups. If the volume and/or efficiency doesn't increase soon, Jefferson's fantasy ceiling will be in trouble.

23-15

The snap difference in the Minnesota backfield prior to Aaron Jones Sr.'s injury, favoring Jordan Mason. The run-heavy nature has helped the Vikings backfield, relying on the volume with their rushing success rate still ranking in the bottom-10. Mason's return in Week 7 was largely the same as Week 1, with each RB getting a near 50/50 split in the carries. I will point out Mason was the surprise leader in routes (11-6) before Jones left with his knee injury, but failed to bring in either of his targets. If Jones does miss time, he reportedly avoided a serious injury Mason can fill his role from Weeks 2-6, averaging 24.3 touches per game and 13.5 fantasy PPG. Next up will be the Detroit Lions, which currently ranks 32nd in total defense.

12

Targets for Tre Tucker, with zero of them being deep balls (targets of 20+ air yards). The one-dimensional vertical threat hasn't been very one-dimensional recently. Sure, that part of his game is still key, but Klint Kubiak has used his WR1 as just that, a WR1. A 7.4 average depth of target is Tucker's lowest on the season, bringing in five of the 12 targets for over 100 yards on Sunday. As long as Kirk Cousins is starting, the raw numbers make him a safer play, as Cousins has over 240 passing yards in each of the last six weeks. Tucker's floor isn't much worse than 90% of flex plays and brings a huge ceiling along with it.

11

Touches for Jonah Coleman, as well as the combined touches for J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey. The rookie wasted no time making an impact in his return from IR as he led the RB room in just about everything: snaps, carries, routes, yards, all of it. After Dobbins got the first three carries of the game, Coleman out-carried Denver's RB1 9-to-3, adding two receptions. Dobbins was saved in this one with a goal-line TD, but going forward, all three are TD-or-bust, with Coleman having the best shot at carving out a weekly fantasy role.

70.8%

Pass rate for the Green Bay Packers in their first game with Josh Jacobs back. The Packers' pass-first attack stayed strong in Week 7, going above its season average with Jordan Love dropping back to pass 46 times. The concern isn't fully washed away; the Lions defense has faced a pass-heavy attack nearly every game because of the unit’s weaknesses, but it gives some confidence that Packers WRs Christian Watson and Matthew Golden will stay as elite options.

Green Bay is bottom-five in yards before contact and two more injuries on the offensive line (Sean Rhyan, Jacob Monk) this week isn't helping its cause. There's been more than just a RB talent issue. The area I do have some concern with is at the goal line, where Love already has five passing touchdowns. Jacobs has been a ball magnet in the past inside the five-yard line.

17.3

PPR PPG for Tee Higgins since 2024 with Joe Burrow, which would rank as the WR6. Tee Higgins is consistently underrated and it's happening again. In the past, he has dealt with plenty of injury issues, but when he and his QB are healthy, Ja'Marr Chase isn't the only fantasy WR1 on the team. This season in particular, Higgins is just inside the top-10 for both half-PPR and PPR leagues, which is more impressive with only two touchdowns so far. In the last two seasons, Higgins' red-zone ability has propelled him to a 10.1% touchdown-per-target rate, and currently only at 4.0% in 2026.

129

Receiving yards for Browns rookie KC Concepcion. Cleveland has tried to get the rookie involved, giving Concepcion a league-high nine designed targets entering Week 7, but it didn't all come together until this Sunday. He had 10 targets, 81 yards after the catch and sadly a dropped TD, though it still turned into a WR1 fantasy day. His yards after the catch are what made the day possible, nearly matching his season total from his first 35 targets. It can be difficult to predict which of the Browns' pass-catchers is worth playing, making me view Concepcion as a bye-week fill-in that has more upside value as a rookie receiver entering the back half of the year.

item.title: Ups and Downs from Saints vs. Steelers
item.description: Not a lot looked good in the Saints loss in Paris.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints were defeated 16-10 by the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday to fall to 2-5. The Saints were hosts to the first game ever in Paris, and unfortunately couldn’t take advantage of the occasion. Not a lot looked good for the Saints in the loss, and there are a lot more questions than answers.

Up: WR Barion Brown

After recording his first NFL reception last week, Barion Brown followed it up with a 3-reception, 57-yard game. Brown was also a factor as a returner, returning a punt for 20 yards and a kick for 42 yards.

With Jordyn Tyson eyeing a potential return after the bye week, the Saints wide receiver depth is hoping to make an impact to earn playtime. With Brown continuing to be a factor and making plays, his snap count may continue to rise despite the return of the team’s eighth overall pick.

Down: Run Game

I mean, come on. Are we serious? The Saints’ run game on Sunday may be the worst I’ve seen in a long time, possibly ever. New Orleans rushed 17 times for 18 yards, with running backs averaging 0.8 yards per carry. This isn’t just a problem at this point; it is becoming an emergency. Even 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers rushed for more yards than any single Saints player.

The Saints’ run game has been a problem since last season, and they’ve poured money into fixing it this offseason. David Edwards has been serviceable at best, and Travis Etienne hasn’t been healthy. But worst of all, the Saints’ run design is plain bad. Running backs are rushing for 0.0 yards before contact, and they have no chance.

Worst of all for New Orleans, their run defense wasn’t able to slow down Pittsburgh at all. The Steelers rushed for 130 more yards than the Saints and dominated the trenches. New Orleans had a major problem last season, and it has failed to improve through seven weeks of the 2026 season.

Down: Kellen Moore

Kellen Moore bought himself some more time after the win over the New York Giants, but a slow and boring loss against the Steelers, where the Saints were totally dominated, keeps him on the hot seat. The Saints are undisciplined, and Moore can’t adjust. The locker room is close to breaking, and the Saints aren’t far off from looking for their next head coach.

Moore may survive the bye week and into the home game against the Cleveland Browns, but another loss, especially in similar fashion in Paris, and the Saints will likely have an interim head coach for the rest of the season.

The Daily Slop – 26 October 2026

Last Man Standig (paywall)

The Jayden Daniels conversation is worth having; everyone will be okay

The third-year QB has played well since rejoining the lineup, but two baffling mistakes, a prolonged winless stretch and questions about his decision-making deserve scrutiny

Something feels off with Jayden Daniels — and it’s okay to discuss why.

This isn’t about questioning whether the third-year player is Washington’s franchise quarterback. He is! Daniels’ potential is what keeps hope alive during tough stretches. The question is why a player whose poise, command and decision-making defined his extraordinary rookie season is suddenly making mistakes and choices that seem so out of character.

I’m talking about game awareness — the clock-management debacle against the Giants in Week 5 and throwing the ball away on fourth down against the 49ers. Two of the season’s most inexplicable plays, in consecutive games, involving a quarterback who previously seemed well beyond such moments.

Questions also linger about Daniels’ aggressiveness in the passing game. Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback Kurt Warner discussed that concern as a recent guest on “Last Man Standig” (video below). The NFL Network analyst was impressed with Daniels’ performance against the 49ers in real time. A closer look at the tape left him wanting more.

But this is about more than two plays or passing up opportunities. The Commanders don’t win anymore.

For more from Ben Standig, click here

Sports Illustrated

Jayden Daniels — “I failed to the standard I hold myself to”

Week 6 — Following the Giants tie

Question: Looking back at the final play against the Giants, did the players realize how much time remained?

“I mean, just going back and reflecting on it and, you know, sitting back and ultimately, I know it’s a lot of he say or whatever you’re trying to make, but ultimately, like, it’s on me at the end. I know DQ is getting a lot of slack for it or whatever, you know, but regardless of what happens, I’m the person on the field that’s supposed to calm everything, control everything, and I failed to the standard I hold myself to and the standard in this organization. So it’s just something for me to move on. Not saying I’m proud of it or anything. Obviously looking back, like, it could have resulted in a loss, we tied, but it was a fail in my eyes and, you know, I know I’m better than that. I hold myself to a higher standard than that.”

At the bye: There has been plenty of criticism directed at Quinn and the coaching staff, but Daniels wasn’t interested in letting them take all the blame. He understood what happened and recognized that he had a responsibility to manage the situation on the field. That’s part of becoming the leader Washington needs him to be. The talent has never been the question with Daniels. How he handles moments like this will help determine what kind of quarterback he becomes.

Commanders Roundtable

Jayden Daniels: A new scheme and growing pains

Under relentless pressure, Daniels has occasionally looked rushed and confused. The constant threat of immediate pressure has accelerated his internal clock, causing him to abandon clean pockets prematurely or scramble before deeper route concepts can develop downfield.

Hall of Fame quarterback and analyst Kurt Warner highlighted this dynamic in his film breakdown, noting that Daniels is occasionally passing up open opportunities downfield. Warner claims that although Daniels has played “good” this season, his lack of aggression is preventing him from being great.

This leads to a larger question: is Daniels becoming too risk-averse?

The analytics back up Warner’s evaluation: PFF logs Daniels’ Big-Time Throw rate (BTT%) at just 2.9%, well below the league average for starters. While his extreme care with the football (0 INTs) protects possession, the low BTT% reveals a tendency to take safe check-downs or pull the ball down to run rather than attacking tight coverage windows.

What I’d like to see after the bye week is a renewed commitment from the coaching staff to protect Daniels in the pocket, alongside Daniels showing the poise to pull the trigger on downfield shots. The designs are producing open receivers on film, even if Blough’s overall sequencing and game feel have drawn criticism. Once Daniels regains comfort in his protection, he can overcome the gun-shy tendencies that have crept into his process.

“In the past, it varies. You would like, as a goal, to be the first quarter of the season, you know, in those first four games. Sometimes it happens faster, like that Game 3, because you’re still working out some of the kinks. Sometimes you’re trying to get the continuity together, especially if you have a lot of new guys. Some things that goes into that. But definitely by the first quarter of the season, you have a good beat on, ‘Okay, this is who we are. This is how our guys respond and how they play.’ And then you can kind of build even from a staff perspective in terms of, you know, we’re still — I know I am — in terms of, you know, you watch these guys in practice and so forth like that, but also, you know, we say practice execution becomes game reality.

So how they respond in games, you kind of understand, ‘Okay, this player is better at that than I thought he was, so let’s utilize him more in that way,’ or, ‘He’s not quite where we want to be in that particular space, so let’s keep him out of those spaces.’ And so I think by the first four games, you kind of have a better idea of the team and the defense as a whole.”

Washington stayed at 1-4-1 on its bye, but New York’s 27-21 overtime win in Houston pushed the Giants to 4-2-1 and made the Commanders’ NFC East climb even steeper

For a Commanders team that has managed only one win, that’s a costly development during a week when it couldn’t do anything to change its own record.

Houston actually gave Washington some late hope. C.J. Stroud connected with Xavier Hutchinson for a touchdown with 52 seconds remaining, tying the game at 21 and forcing overtime.

But the Texans went three-and-out on their opening overtime possession. New York needed only two offensive plays to end it, with Cam Skattebo breaking a 42-yard run before Devin Singletary scored from 30 yards out.

For Commanders fans rooting against the Giants, that was about as frustrating an ending as possible.

Look at where this leaves Washington. The Commanders come off the bye at a disadvantage in the division without having lost a game in the meantime. They’ll need wins of their own, obviously, but they’ll also need the rest of the league to start beating New York, and they’ll need the Monday night result to break their way.

Peters has shown financial restraint, knowing some big extensions are due. Daniels is the most important, and even though Year 4 on the deal will be relatively modest at $12.01 million, it will be the last season it’s cheap.

This is a problem.

There is real urgency to make the roster better around Daniels. He’s proven to be the franchise guy, and if he stays healthy the rest of the way, Washington would be wise to pay him what he’s asking.

But that doesn’t make it any less complicated to mold a team capable of challenging deep into the playoffs.

It’s a dangerous cycle. The schedule gets easier after the bye week, but the pressure to produce remains. Daniels has already proven he can drive this team forward, but doing that on more than $50 million per year is different from his $10.29 million cap hit this season.

Washington is in a precarious situation. Paying Daniels is easy; what comes next is the tricky part.

Roob’s Observations: Why a Howie Roseman trade deadline sell-off is unlikely

I keep hearing about all the players Howie is going to unload before the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10. Guys like Saquon Barkley, Moro Ojomo, Zack Baun, Riq Woolen, Landon Dickerson and Dallas Goedert. Basically, older players who may not fit into the Eagles’ future or players on the final year of their contract situation who may be unsignable. Don’t count on it.

While a sell-off is possible if this thing continues to spiral, there’s two important things to remember. First of all, you’re never going to trade a player for less or equal what he might bring you in the comp pick equation. Moro Ojomo for example is probably going to bring you a 3rd-round comp pick and you’re not going to get a 2nd-rounder for him. Howie Roseman values picks the same whether they’re a year later, so he’d rather have a comp 3rd-round pick in 2028 than a 4th-round pick in 2027.

The second thing to remember is that in the current NFC East landscape, there’s a chance the Eagles will still be in the playoff race when the trade deadline arrives on Nov. 10. They have the Cowboys, Commanders and Giants before the deadline, combined record 6-10-1. And 0-7-1 vs. teams with a winning record. So as grim as things look right now, they look just as grim for everyone else in the division, and if the Eagles win two of these next three Howie isn’t going to start selling off pieces at 4-5. He owes it to Jeff Lurie and the players and coaches and the city to keep the team intact if the Eagles are in contact with the division leaders.

item.title: Report: NFL "furious" over Eagles' handling of the Jalen Hurts messaging
item.description: The NFL reportedly has no issue with the manner in which the Eagles handled the health of quarterback Jalen Hurts in London.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL reportedly has no issue with the manner in which the Eagles handled the health of quarterback Jalen Hurts in London. In contrast, the league is not thrilled with the manner in which the team handled the ensuing controversy.

Marcus Hayes of the Philadelphia Inquirer, citing an unnamed "longtime source well-connected to the NFL offices," reports that the powers-that-be are "furious" with the team for its messaging regarding the situation.

To date, only coach Nick Sirianni has been made available to answer the obvious follow-up questions raised by a pair of statements issued by the team. Sirianni didn't have much to say, regardless of whether he did (or didn't) know more about the matter than he shared.

G.M. Howie Roseman, who runs the entire football operation, has not addressed the issue. The doctors who evaluated Hurts have not been made available.

Through it all, the team has hidden behind "patient privacy" — even after the statements shared specific details about the "superficial" blood clot that became a deep vein thrombosis and multiple blood clots in his lungs. The medical privacy rights of Jalen Hurts have already been compromised, if not expressly waived. Specific questions about how the initial condition arose, when it was diagnosed, how it was treated, and whether the complications flowed from those decisions are irrelevant at this point to the issue of privacy.

Of course, the NFL didn't help the situation via the dismissive comments made by multiple executives last week, including chief medical officer Allen Sills. His insistence that Hurts had "very conservative" care doesn't mesh on the surface with the decision to let him fly to London, to play in London, and to fly home from London.

On Sunday, the NFL and NFL Players Association jointly announced that they are "working together" on the Hurts case. It's unclear what that means, especially since the NFLPA has not yet officially invoked its unilateral right to demand an investigation under Article 39, Section 5(f) of the Collective Bargaining Agreement.

The union can't afford the perception of complicity in a possible coverup. Any investigation, in whatever form it takes, must seek real answers to hard questions and provide them to the public.

It's impossible for the NFL to, on one hand, welcome public attention, engagement, and stadium funding while, on the other, say "none of your damn business" when the public has natural curiosity about the things that happen to NFL players. Last week, the Eagles failed to satisfy the widespread interest in Hurts's case. Moving forward, any effort to investigate what happened must include a commitment to true and complete transparency.

Through it all, the Eagles play a home game tonight against the Cowboys. It will be interesting to see whether and to what extent ESPN's wall-to-wall coverage of the game advances the lingering Hurts story.

It's impossible for the NFL to, on one hand, welcome public attention, engagement, and stadium funding while, on the other, say "none of your damn business" when the public has natural curiosity about the things that happen to NFL players. Last week, the Eagles failed to satisfy the widespread interest in Hurts's case. Moving forward, any effort to investigate what happened must include a commitment to true and complete transparency.

Through it all, the Eagles play a home game tonight against the Cowboys. It will be interesting to see whether and to what extent ESPN's wall-to-wall coverage of the game advances the lingering Hurts story.

item.title: Packers Injury Updates: Sean Rhyan, Zaire Franklin likely to miss time
item.description: The hits just keep coming and the Packers’ injury report just keeps growing.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers got some unpleasant news on the injury front on Monday morning following the team’s 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 7. Two starters, one in the middle of each of the offense and defense, are likely to miss more time with injuries, though neither one is expected to be season-ending.

First up is linebacker Zaire Franklin, who was ruled out for Sunday’s game after suffering a leg injury in practice during the week. Ian Rapoport of NFL Network reports that Franklin has a hairline fracture in his leg, which explains why he was unable to play in Week 7. That injury will likely keep him out for the Packers’ Week 8 game against the Panthers on Thursday Night Football, but the team is not expected to put him on injured reserve.

On the other side of the football, it appears likely that starting center Sean Rhyan will head to IR. Rapoport is on the Rhyan injury as well, and it is believed to be a high ankle sprain. Rhyan is fortunate to have avoided any fractures, but he still could be looking at a month-plus for recovery time, which could line up with a stint on injured reserve.

Green Bay also lost backup center Jacob Monk to an injury just a few plays after Rhyan left the game, meaning John Williams had to enter the game as an emergency option. He performed admirably for the most part, and could be in line to start on Thursday against Carolina if Monk is also unavailable on a short week.

The decision not to shut Franklin down suggests that the Packers expect him to return to the field before the end of November. Had they put him on IR, he would need to sit for the next four games before being eligible to return to the active roster. Should either of these injured players actually go on injured reserve, they would be ineligible to return until the game against the New Orleans Saints in Week 13, due to the Packers’ bye coming in Week 11.

item.title: Chiefs Week 7 snap count analysis: L’Jarius Sneed has less playing time
item.description: Here are the important notes from Kansas City’s snap-count breakdown in the Week 7 loss.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis!

Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs’ snap counts in the 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in Week 7. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats.

Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Joshua Ezeudu, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Jalen Royals, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray

Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, LB Jack Cochrane, CB Mansoor Delane, CB Nohl Williams, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner

Did not play: QB Justin Fields, OT Diego Pounds

Inactive: QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), DB Jadon Canady, FB Ben VanSumeren, DE Jack Pyburn, WR Rashee Rice (Hamstring) and OT Jaylon Moore (concussion)

The big takeaway: L’Jarius Sneed plays a season-low 14 snaps

Early and often, the Seahawks offense attacked Chiefs’ slot cornerback L’Jarius Sneed by throwing over the middle to wide receivers Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Cooper Kupp. Pro Football Focus says Sneed allowed five catches for 83 yards and four first downs.

Anecdotally, it felt like the Chiefs adjusted the lineup to exclude Sneed as the game went on, and the snap counts back that up. Sneed played just 14 snaps (11 coverage snaps), just 20% of the defense’s total snap volume.

Safety Chris Roland-Wallace (31 snaps) led the team in reps at slot cornerback, lining up there seven more times than Sneed. Roland-Wallace allowed three catches for 15 yards on three targets.

It was the least playing time Sneed has had in a single game this season. The matchup was tough for Kansas City’s secondary, but Sneed especially struggled against the slot. The next time the Chiefs face high-end slot receiving talent like Seattle’s, the plan may look different.

The Offensive takeaway: Cyrus Allen leads wideouts in production

The Chiefs’ wideouts combined for 39 receiving yards on 13 targets.

  • Xavier Worthy (46 snaps): 11 yards on 6 targets
  • Jalen Royals (36 snaps): 0 yards on 2 targets
  • Andrew Armstrong (31 snaps): 3 yards on 2 targets
  • Cyrus Allen (16 snaps): 18 yards on 2 targets
  • Justin Watson (5 snaps): 7 yards on 1 target

The fifth-round rookie Allen, who saw the field for just 11 pass plays in Seattle, outproduced the rest of the room with one catch.

The Seahawks’ defense suffocated the Chiefs’ passing attack, and quarterback Patrick Mahomes offered little relief, missing a handful of throws, but it’s the second time this season Kansas City’s wide receiver corps got basically shut out. In Week 1, the Chiefs ran to victory over the Denver Broncos, but the pass game needed to step up this week and didn’t.

The Defensive takeaway: R Mason Thomas’ playing time decreases

After rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas played as many as 50 snaps at times this season, he played just 20 of the defense’s reps against Seattle, a season-low mark for the second-round pick. He was on the field for 15 pass plays, dropping into coverage on three.

Thomas was on the field for just five run plays, which matches the four times he played against the run against the Los Angeles Chargers last week. Since the bye week, Thomas’ usage has shifted more toward pass downs than in Weeks 3 and 4.

Against the Seahawks, Thomas registered four pressures, including a quarterback hit, coming off of five against the Chargers. The first-year edge rusher may be settling into a more pass-down-only role while defensive ends Felix Anudike-Uzomah (19 run snaps) and Ashton Gillotte (28 run snaps) handle most of the every-down duties.

item.title: Eagles News: Saquon Barkley trade scenarios include … the Giants
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 10/26/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

I don’t think the Giants will be trading for Saquon Barkley. But the G-Men sure could be buyers as they currently approach the NFL trade deadline with an NFC East lead.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

Saquon Barkley trade proposals: Six deals Eagles could consider, including stunning Giants reunion – CBS Sports

Giants receive: Saquon Barkley … Eagles receive: Cam Skattebo, 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pick … In such a weak NFC East, the division-leading Giants have a path to the playoffs, but they need a functional run game to get there. Even with their abundance of options, it seems John Harbaugh does not know who to deploy at running back (especially if you ask Najee Harris). Reuniting with Barkley eliminates all questions. Plus, Harbaugh himself said this week that it would be “great” to be in a “Saquon Barkley circumstance” where the Giants had a clear-cut No. 1 ballcarrier. A return to New York makes plenty of sense for Barkley, but it would likely cost the Giants a premium to pull it off, given the intra-division nature of the trade. For multiple years of control of the Eagles’ star running back, they may have to part with their own top running back asset in addition to meaningful draft capital.

Eagles vs. Cowboys Week 7 game information – BGN

The Philadelphia Eagles are now 2-4 heading into their Week 7 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys on Monday Night Football, and both NFC East teams desperately need a win. Expectations have changed a lot for the Eagles, whose list of injured players includes nearly half of the active 53-man roster, but this is still a rivalry game in Philadelphia on Monday night. It might not be the same as when Jalen Hurts greets the team out of the tunnel, but they are getting some guys back, including Saquon Barkley.

‘Other’ potentially outgoing Eagles players who make sense as trade bait – PhillyVoice

RG Tyler Steen (26). Why should the Eagles trade him? Steen is scheduled to be a free agent next offseason, and the Eagles may not be willing to afford what he could be paid on the open market. Note: Steen is a more valuable trade chip than Landon Dickerson, in my opinion, but we didn’t include him in the original batch of valuable, tradable players on the premise that the Eagles would need him just to get through the season. But that was before it was revealed that Jalen Hurts was done for the season. Now? “Getting through this season” isn’t quite as important. Why should other teams trade for him? There are always teams in desperate need of offensive line help, and Steen is a decent enough starter. Trade value: Fourth- and sixth-round picks.

Breaking down Cowboys-Eagles MNF matchup in wide-open NFC East – ESPN

Nick Sirianni has a 61-28 record since taking over as coach in Philadelphia, has led the team to five playoff appearances in as many seasons and has gotten to the Super Bowl twice, winning one of them. You’d think he’d have a good bit of equity built up. That’s being tested in 2026 with the Eagles in a four-game skid, dropping their record to 5-9 over the past 14 games dating to last season. Sirianni’s in-game decision-making has had a hand in the current losing streak, though a depleted roster hit by injury, retirement (Lane Johnson) and trade (Cam Jurgens) is the primary culprit. The offense is lost right now and has had its share of issues during his tenure. Sirianni is a former offensive coordinator but the Eagles have outsourced a good chunk of those responsibilities, with mixed results. If they hit on their offensive coordinator, the team tends to have great success and that OC often moves on to become a head coach. If they miss, the offense sags, the OC gets let go and they’re back on the merry-go-round. It remains to be seen if that’s a ride management wants to continue to sign up for.

Eagles-Cowboys questions: More on the Jalen Hurts saga, Saquon Barkley’s return – The Athletic

Berman: My prevailing takeaway is that the Cowboys have the talent advantage. In the past five years, there haven’t been many times when you felt the Eagles entered games with inferior personnel, but injuries and exits have made that the Eagles’ reality. That will be the difference Monday. Both teams are struggling and underperforming. Both teams badly need a win. I don’t see enough offensive firepower from the Eagles, and I’m not sure they’ll have enough of a pass rush to limit the Cowboys. The path to a win is a strong ground game to control the clock and Vic Fangio’s unit pressuring Dak Prescott and limiting Dallas to field goals. The Eagles have lost four straight and are home underdogs for a reason. A bad season gets worse Monday. Cowboys 24, Eagles 21

NFL, NFLPA are “working together” to review Jalen Hurts situation – PFT

As another full Sunday of football approaches, there’s a new development in the situation regarding Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is likely out for the rest of the year after a “superficial” blood clot became a deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in each lung. “The NFL and NFL Players Association are working together to review the matter,” the league and the union said in a joint statement. This implies that the NFLPA, as mentioned earlier today, has not yet officially exercised its unilateral right to conduct an investigation under Article 39, Section 5(f) of the Collective Bargaining Agreement. Still, some sort of an investigation is inevitable.

How Kenny Moore II gained perspective in a unique offseason – NBCSP

Kenny Moore II grew up loving scrapbooks. He loved seeing pictures on the wall. He loved creating that art. Truth be told, he wanted to be a photographer. Then he became a professional football player and that’s a good life too. But he missed photography. “In the football environment, I put the camera down,” Moore said a few weeks ago, “because I felt like art and sports were just not a thing, like you shouldn’t do this. So I did that for a couple years. Because I put myself in a space that football is all that matters.” In the last year, Moore has picked up the camera again. He’s still a motivated NFL football player and has already cracked the Eagles’ starting lineup after joining the team last month. He still wants to be the best version of himself he can be between the white lines. But he refuses to be only that. He wants to be much more. There’s something healthy about that.

NFL Week 7 Bets: Matchups to target – PFF

And while the sample size is small for Tanner McKee, he has struggled against disruption throughout his career, particularly against perfect coverage, where he has lost nearly 0.75 EPA per play across his 150 total career dropbacks. Betting tips: I’ll be targeting Eagles team total unders, Dallas alternate spreads and parlays featuring plenty of sacks and turnovers by Philadelphia’s offense.

Why the Eagles Are In Salary Cap Trouble, and How They Can Get Out of It – SI

And that brings us to the other way this strategy can be stressed: by an unexpected injury, decline or retirement from a key player. In this case, it was Carson Wentz, who got a record-breaking contract in early 2019, and fell apart thereafter, in part due to an accumulation of injuries. Long story short, the Eagles traded Wentz, which meant (unlike a post–June 1 cut), they had to take all his dead money at once, and that $33.8 million accounted for a large percentage of the $59 million (or so) in total dead money they carried that year. With the lower limit, that meant roughly a third of Philly’s cap was occupied by players who weren’t on the team. That team started 3–6, then rallied to finish 9–8 and sneak in the playoffs. So what was the fix? The Eagles drafted well, got really young and developed a rising layer of young players to supplement an older core. In their playoff loss to the Buccaneers that season, their quarterback and every single skill player who touched the ball was on a rookie contract. And with the cap cleaned out after they ate dead money for a year, they got aggressive in 2022, acquiring guys like Brown, Haason Reddick, C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Robert Quinn (Quinn shows these moves don’t all work out), and made the Super Bowl. This year, they’ve faced some similar unforeseen circumstances. Lane Johnson, their all-world tackle of 14 seasons, retired. The Ravens offered a second-round pick for Cam Jurgens, capital that could be used to get younger (like the capital in the Wentz trade once was), and they couldn’t say no. Hurts’s blood clots, first discovered before the team’s London game and found to be more serious last week, will likely sideline him for the rest of 2026. The season’s gone sideways. Maybe they can win a wounded NFC East. Maybe not. Their next steps, either way, will be interesting.

A special message to Eagles fans from Jeffrey Lurie – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

To Eagles fans everywhere, My induction into the Eagles Hall of Fame will always be a moment I look back on with immense pride. To join such a legendary group of individuals who have helped shape this franchise is an incredible honor and one that fills me with gratitude. Throughout my career, I’ve had the good fortune of working alongside some extraordinary people whose contributions have been instrumental to our team’s success. To our coaches, players, and front office to everyone who has proudly represented this organization, I am deeply grateful for your dedication, commitment, and shared pursuit of excellence.

Giants-Texans ‘things I think’: The Giants are in it to win it – Big Blue View

That was New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh after Sunday’s stunning 27-21 overtime victory over the Houston Texans. The words got my attention. Because they, stunningly, feel like the truth. The Giants are 4-2-1 and leading the NFC East. They will still be leading the division after the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys, both 2-4, play on Monday Night Football. The outside world can, and will, snicker at the NFC East. They can, and will, snicker at the Giants. It is hard to blame them. The Eagles have had a stunning fall. They are without Jalen Hurts for the remainder of the season, and the situation surrounding his blood clots could embarrass both the Eagles and the NFL. They have myriad injuries beyond Hurts, and an offensive line that does not resemble the dominant one they possessed not long ago.

J.J. McCarthy’s redemption arc is bad news for the Vikings – SB Nation

There’s an inherent risk in anointing anyone as “back” based on a single game; we all know this. It’s also impossible to ignore that J.J. McCarthy marched the Giants offense into Houston, and dismantled the defense without it looking particularly difficult. It wasn’t always pretty from McCarthy, especially late in the game — but that didn’t matter. When the dust settled, he still finished 20-for-28, and 272 yards. Touchdowns eluded McCarthy, but critically so did interceptions. What he did was exactly what a John Harbaugh quarterback needs to do: manage what he could, didn’t overextend, and controlled the game to the point the defense and run game could carry them over the line. There are unquestionably things McCarthy still needs to work on. While his short passing over the middle of the field was good, he’s still not comfortable throwing deep into the middle and threading the ball against high safety coverage. The Giants’ QB only attempted four passes in the middle third of the field, only one of which was completed for 10+ yards. This is a skill he needs to develop in order to become a complete quarterback, because making comfortable outside throws with beneficial leverage is only part of playing the position in the NFL. The Texans used a strategy that took the middle of the field away, but there were still opportunities left on the table. Middle field plays are where teams most often generate explosives through YAC, and ignoring that will stifle the offensive potential of the Giants. Nevertheless, the team won. It was a big win, a signature win — and helps cement New York as a team to watch in the East.

5 things to watch when the Cowboys play the Eagles – Blogging The Boys

Don’t get complacent. With the Eagles’ offense visibly short-handed and struggling, the Cowboys have no excuse not to seize total control of this game right from the onset. Unfortunately, dominating in any fashion has simply not been the Cowboys’ way. They start games remarkably slow, and unnecessarily set the stage for an intense, frantic finish. If the Cowboys allow that sluggish script to play out again, this game will be destined for another frustrating evening. What will be incredibly frustrating to watch is if this turns into a boring, low-scoring affair where the Cowboys’ offense becomes completely complacent because they feel the punchless Eagles simply don’t possess the firepower to make any type of push. That is stinkin’ thinkin’ because the Cowboys’ defense is not reliable enough to safely protect a lead and could completely fall apart at any moment. The offense must attack, establish a lead, and keep attacking if they want to leave Philadelphia with a commendable, respected showing.

Tyler’s Take – Is Commanders GM Adam Peters using Dan Quinn as his fall guy? – Hogs Haven

There is ZERO doubt in my mind that Adam Peters wants this to be his team and he probably views head coach Dan Quinn as a dead man walking, which is why he may be, as Candi subtly hints, meddling. Is Adam Peters using Dan Quinn as his “fall guy”? Does he TRULY believe his players are not the problem and it’s more on the coaches?
