item.title: Giants-Texans: 5 key plays in New York’s victory over Houston
item.description: The Giants upset the Texans and improve to 4-2-1. Here are five plays that led to that outcome.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants shocked the Houston Texans on Sunday in J.J. McCarthy’s first start with John Harbaugh. New York controlled the game on offense and defense, defeating the Texans, 27-21 in overtime. 

Dennard Wilson’s defense held the high-powered passing attack 153 yards through the air, as Houston gained just 237 total yards. Tae Banks shut down Nico Collins, Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud looked uncomfortable, and D.J. Reader continued to be a strong asset for the Giants both as a run defender and a pass rusher.

The Giants’ offense incorporated a lot of PISTOL concepts and zone-read runs that helped to open up the rushing attack. McCarthy’s two 40+ yard passing plays in the first quarter helped to soften the box, as did the threat of his legs on read plays.

New York gained 420 yards on offense. McCarthy threw for 252 yards, and, most notably, the rushing attack got going for 188 yards on the ground with an average of 5.5 yards per carry.

Houston ranked third in the league in run defense prior to the game, and the Giants were 19th in rushing with three straight poor performances. The return of Jermaine Eleumunor certainly helped, but the Giants – in general – deserve a lot of credit for this complete effort, other than the poor kicking by Dominic Zvada. Here are five plays, or five sequences of plays, that were impactful in the game.

Play(s) 1: Final two plays of the game

The Giants have been bad at running the football over the last few games. The running backs were publicly called out by John Harbaugh, and Cam Skattebo played six snaps against the Saints. Skattebo responded, rushing for 124 yards on 17 carries with a touchdown. The vindication of the overall running game was best represented by the final two plays of overtime:

Skattebo rushed for 42 yards on the second play of overtime, which set up Devin Singletary’s 30-yard touchdown run to match the Giants’ win total from last season. New York now has confidence heading into a much-needed bye week. 

Play(s) 2: End of the first half

The Giants were ahead by points with 3:32 left in the first half and Stroud marched down the field 90 yards to find Marvin Harrison Jr. for a touchdown, along with a two-point conversion on a shovel pass to Cade Stover:

Arguably, the most significant play of the drive was a 43-yard catch and run to Tank Dell (welcome back). The ball didn’t even appear intended for Dell, but it was significant for Houston. 

Dru Phillips and Ar’Darius Washington were flagged to help extend the drive; the flags totaled for 32 yards. I love that Harbaugh called his timeouts to give the Giants an opportunity to score points in the waning seconds of the half. It’s great to see the Giants have confidence in McCarthy in that situation. McCarthy connected with Malik Nabers for 27 yards, which put the Giants in field goal range. 

It was excellent coaching by the Giants, but, unfortunately, rookie kicker Dominic Zvada missed the 44-yard field goal and the half ended in a tie. New York dominated this game but it still ended in overtime – Zvada’s struggles were a big reason why. 

Play(s) 3: Excellent start

The Giants had an excellent opening drive that resulted in a nine-play, 66-yard touchdown drive that included a few quality runs, a fourth-down conversion, and a 42-yard completion to Malik Nabers. McCarthy’s athletic ability kept the edge rusher honest and allowed Tyrone Tracy Jr. to hit the hole for a touchdown. 

New York needed a quick start on the road with a young new quarterback and they received exactly that. The defense responded with two early three-and-outs, a few pressures for Abdul Carter in the first three drives, and they dictated with a zone based defense, while also forcing several penalties on the Texans’ offense. 

Play(s) 4: Welcome back, Cam Skattebo!

The Giants went on a 14-play, 80-yard drive that ended in a 16-yard touchdown run by Skattebo:

Skattebo received six snaps in last week’s loss and, by all accounts, he responded excellently in practice. McCarthy ran the Matt Nagy offense well. His third-and-9 conversion to Malachi Fields set up Skattebo’s touchdown. McCarthy delivered an impressively placed out route. The Giants also converted a third-and-1 earlier in the drive to Skattebo on a fake tush-push with Jameis Winston in the game:

Play(s) 5: The struggles of Dominic Zvada 

The Giants rookie kicker missed a 56-yard field goal that would have given the Giants a 10-point lead at the end of the first quarter. After that, John Harbaugh used his timeouts excellently to end the first half. McCarthy completed a 27-yard pass to Nabers with 29 seconds left in the half, putting the Giants in a position to go up three at halftime.

Zvada lined up for a 44-yard field goal in a dome and sent it wide right. The Giants forgoed a field-goal attempt later in the game, resulting in 23 yards of difference after punting the football to the 14-yard line. Luckily, the defense was stellar in the game, and they forced one of their many three and outs.

These struggles are noteworthy, of course, and they almost led the Giants to a devastating loss; Giant fans know too well how those situations can go. Still, Harbaugh gave Zvada a vote of confidence after the game, but it remains a situation worth monitoring.

item.title: Looking Back at the Biggest Trades of the Miami Dolphins’ Rebuild
item.description: From Jaylen Waddle to Jaelan Phillips, revisiting the biggest moves of Miami's rebuild one year later.
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to team-building, sometimes you just can’t beat a trade. Need to get younger? Make a trade! Need a veteran for a playoff push? Make a trade! Want to desperately catch lightning in a bottle by acquiring a former first-round quarterback bust? Trade your <wince> second-round pick to Arizona! (I see you, Josh Rosen. I wish I didn’t.)

Over the past year, the Dolphins have aggressively reshaped their roster, trading away established veterans, former first-round picks and even future Hall of Famer Quinn Ewers in an effort to accelerate the rebuild. With another deadline approaching, let’s revisit the biggest deals of the past 12 months and see how they’re working out so far.

November 2025: Jaelan Phillips

The Deal

Dolphins traded EDGE Jaelan Phillips for the Eagles’ 2026 third-round pick (No. 87), which was used to select TE Will Kacmarek.

The Financial Impact

After finishing the season with the Eagles, Phillips signed a massive four-year, $120 million contract with the Carolina Panthers this offseason, including $80 million guaranteed.

How Phillips Has Performed

After nearly five full seasons in South Florida, where he recorded 177 tackles and 26 sacks, Phillips managed just 28 tackles and two sacks in eight games with Philadelphia. So far in 2026, he has 2.5 sacks and 10 tackles, though he does lead the Panthers with 18 pressures. Stop me if you’ve heard this one before, but Phillips has also missed time with an injury, suffering a hamstring injury in Week 4 before re-aggravating it after the bye.

How Kacmarek Has Performed

Kacmarek, who was drafted primarily for his run-blocking ability, has largely delivered in that role. After a somewhat slow start, he posted PFF grades north of 70 against Kansas City and Minnesota before turning in a more pedestrian performance against Cincinnati.

Early Verdict

You’ll recall Phillips called being traded to Philadelphia “the best thing that’s ever happened” to him. Rude. Still, most of us agreed at the time that a long-term, big-money extension carried significant risk. Turning a player you weren’t likely to re-sign into a third-round pick was sound business. You can debate whether Miami reached for a blocking tight end at No. 87, but there’s something to be said for building a nasty offensive line, and Kacmarek helps you do that. For now, I’m good with it.

March 2026: Minkah Fitzpatrick

The Deal

Dolphins traded S Minkah Fitzpatrick for the Jets’ 2026 seventh-round pick (No. 238), which was used to select EDGE Max Llewellyn.

The Financial Impact

Immediately following the trade, Fitzpatrick signed a three-year, $40 million contract with the Jets.

How Fitzpatrick Has Performed

So far in 2026, Fitzpatrick is doing Fitzpatrick things. He’s recorded 26 tackles, an interception and two passes defended while posting a 73.8 PFF grade. Nine years into his career, the five-time Pro Bowler and three-time All-Pro still looks like one of the better safeties in football.

How Llewellyn Has Performed

Well, he hasn’t been released yet, and if you’re a seventh-round pick, that’s a good sign. Llewellyn received five snaps against the 49ers, two on defense and three on special teams, and currently resides on the practice squad.

Early Verdict

Before the trade, I hoped the Dolphins would do with Fitzpatrick what they did with Jordyn Brooks and keep a proven veteran around as part of the rebuild. If you’re looking to build a secondary of Minkahs, it helps to have the real Minkah on the roster to learn from. So while I understand it, I don’t love that Fitzpatrick was traded. I really don’t love that the return was only a seventh-round pick. And I really, really don’t love that he was traded to the Jets. But when a team commits to a rebuild, sometimes even popular veterans become cap casualties.

March 2026: Jaylen Waddle

The Deal

Dolphins traded WR Jaylen Waddle and a 2026 fourth-round pick (No. 111) for the Broncos’ 2026 first-round pick (No. 30), third-round pick (No. 94) and fourth-round pick (No. 130). After subsequent trades involving the 49ers, the transaction ultimately became Waddle and picks No. 90 and No. 111 for CB Chris Johnson, WR Chris Bell, LB Trey Moore and S Kyle Louis.

The Financial Impact

In May 2024, Waddle signed a three-year, $84.75 million extension that included $76 million guaranteed and kept him under contract through 2028. The Broncos absorbed the entire contract, though the Dolphins incurred a $26.3 million dead-cap charge in 2026 while receiving a $3 million cap credit in 2027. Meanwhile, Johnson, Bell, Moore and Louis are all playing on rookie deals.

How Waddle Has Performed

Much to the surprise of many, including one fantasy football manager (who shall remain nameless) who selected Bo Nix to lead his team, Denver’s offense has been a complete mess this season, and Waddle’s production has suffered along with it. Through five games, he has 22 receptions for 228 yards and one touchdown. A cynic might point out those are WR1 numbers for the Dolphins, but they’re almost certainly not what Denver envisioned when it acquired him.

How Johnson Has Performed

Chris Johnson has been every bit as good as Dolphins fans could have hoped. He has a Minkah-esque 31 tackles, two passes defended and a forced fumble. After a slow start against the Raiders and 49ers, he’s been outstanding, highlighted by an 86.9 PFF grade against Minnesota in Week 5. Teammate Jacob Rodriguez may be getting most of the Defensive Rookie of the Year buzz, but Johnson has a legitimate case of his own.

How Bell Has Performed

Bell was widely viewed as a first-round talent who slid because of injury concerns. The expectation was that he’d miss much of the season while recovering from ACL surgery, yet he’s already appeared in all five games. The numbers (five catches for 92 yards) aren’t eye-popping, but given the injury and his limited time working with Malik Willis, the future still looks bright.

How Moore and Louis Have Performed

Unfortunately, both are currently on injured reserve. Moore suffered a severe ankle injury during the preseason, while Louis sustained an MCL sprain in Week 1 against the Raiders. Louis’ practice window has opened, and expectations are that both players will return later this season.

Early Verdict

Even if Waddle’s disappointing production is largely a byproduct of Denver’s dysfunctional offense, this trade looks like an early win for Miami. The Dolphins shed a major financial commitment and turned the return into several intriguing young players. Chris Johnson alone is making this deal look favorable, and if Bell, Louis and Moore become meaningful contributors, the trade could have a lasting impact on the franchise’s trajectory. Of course, Waddle hasn’t suddenly forgotten how to play wide receiver, and this isn’t necessarily a win-or-lose transaction. But from Miami’s perspective, it’s hard not to like the early returns.

August 2026: Quinn Ewers

The Deal

Dolphins traded QB Quinn Ewers for the Jaguars’ 2028 sixth-round pick.

The Financial Impact

Minimal. Ewers remains on his rookie contract and is not scheduled to become a free agent until 2029.

How Ewers Has Performed

Ewers currently serves as Trevor Lawrence’s backup in Jacksonville and, like most backup quarterbacks, hasn’t seen meaningful game action.

Early Verdict

If Ewers eventually develops into a legitimate NFL starter, Miami may look back on this one with some regret. For now, though, turning a seventh-round pick who didn’t appear to have a future on the roster into a future sixth-round pick qualifies as good business.

So, Was It Worth It?

If nothing else, these trades illustrate just how aggressive Miami has been in reshaping its roster. Established veterans, former stars, fan favorites, draft picks and future cap space have all been put on the table. Whether the Dolphins ultimately move Austin Jackson, Josh Uche, Zach Sieler or someone else before November 10, recent history suggests one thing: Nobody is untouchable if the front office believes the return helps accelerate the rebuild.

One broader takeaway is that these moves aren’t simply about moving older veterans for younger talent. Minkah is 29. Waddle and Phillips are 27. These are productive players in their prime, and Miami still chose to move them in exchange for 21- and 22-year-olds. Agree or disagree with any individual trade, I appreciate that the new regime in Miami isn’t interested in half-measures. Turning this team into a perennial playoff contender requires conviction – so far, Jon-Eric Sullivan looks like he understands the assignment.

item.title: Packers Winners and Losers: Week 7 vs. the Lions
item.description: The Packers left much to be desired after a loss to one of their biggest rivals.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers are officially 4-3 after a frustrating last-second 20-17 loss to the division rival Detroit Lions. The offense continued to suffer from another case of the dropsies, Jordan Love lost two more offensive linemen, and the refs…the refs! Let’s dive into this weekend’s winners and losers.

Winner: Jordan Love

QB Jordan Love is once again making do while the world falls apart around him. After starting C Sean Rhyan went down with an injury in the first quarter, Jacob Monk subbed in and…also left the game with an injury. Like, almost immediately after. Did you guys know John Williams played center? Does John Williams know he plays center? Love was running for his life on Sunday, and still able to make some incredible plays in the process, like his gorgeous TD pass to TE Tucker Kraft in the first quarter.

With almost no time to throw, he was somehow able to get this one to WR Savion Williams on 4th and 5. Later in the game, he had another gorgeous throw to WR Christian Watson on 4th and 3.

Along with the pocket collapsing around him, Love had to deal with the drops. THE DROPS. This time it was Bo Melton and Josh Jacobs getting into the act. Jacobs’ drop, in particular, cost the team a go-ahead touchdown.

Love finished the game 27 for 45 (60%) for 274 yards, 2 TD, 1 INT, and 0 roughing the passer calls.

Winner: Javon Bullard

The Packers safety continues to impress this season. He had some great coverage on WR Amon-Ra St. Brown to force an incompletion on 3rd and 17, and the Lions punted as a result. Later in the game, he tackled St. Brown for a big loss on a jet sweep, a play which otherwise might’ve done some damage to the Packers in years past. Bullard is playing like a stud in 2026. He finished the game with 2 total tackles and 1 PD.

Winner: Evan Williams

Lions QB Jared Goff has yet to throw a pick this season, and S Evan Williams came close to changing that, twice. The drops from the offense unfortunately carried over to the defense, because Williams dropped both of his near-picks. That’ll be the big story about Williams’ play from Sunday, but he was disruptive all over the field, as he has been all year. Williams finished the day with 9 total tackles and 1 PD. All-Pro season: still on.

Loser: Matthew Golden

WR Matthew Golden has blossomed into one of Jordan Love’s favorite targets, and for good reason. Golden is a playmaker, and he’s hard to beat without getting called for PI. Love targeted Golden a game-high 12 times on Sunday but he caught just 6 of 12 targets for 39 yards. He had some really great plays, like his first quarter catch below, but the drops continue to stain the Packers offense in 2026, and they need to be fixed, fast.

Loser: Josh Jacobs

The RB finished the day with 11 carries for 36 yards, 5 catches for 55 yards, and 1 TD. He also pled no contest to battery in September after a May 2026 incident involving his former girlfriend and dropped a go-ahead touchdown. Yikes.

Loser: Trey Smack

Brandon McManus, I order you to stop haunting my rookie kicker’s body immediately. Smack was absolutely atrocious on Sunday, ruining what was otherwise a pretty nice opening drive for the Packers offense when he missed a 26 yard FG. Later in the game (and exactly one play after Jacobs’ drop), he missed a 35 yarder after it looked like a Lions player got a hand on it. 6 points left on the field by the kicker. The Packers lost by 3 points. Math is fun (derogatory.)

The Packers have a short week as they head back home to face off against the 3-3 Carolina Panthers, who just got blown out by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this weekend. The Panthers have given the Packers a bit of trouble in recent years: they beat them 16-13 in 2025, and nearly beat them on Christmas Eve during their 2023 meeting (with a 2-12 record!) Can the Packers right the ship with just a couple days off? Find out on Thursday Night Football.

item.title: 'Frustrated' Kenneth Walker III didn't shake hands with Seahawks after Chiefs' loss
item.description: Seattle Seahawks safety Nick Emmanwori said he had extra motivation to stop former teammate Kenneth Walker on "Sunday Night Football."
item.content:encoded:
Nick Emmanwori was not shy about expressing the extra motivation he felt going into the "Sunday Night Football" game on Oct. 25.

The Seattle Seahawks safety told reporters after Seattle's 20-3 win over the Kansas City Chiefs that he wanted to shut down former teammate – and current Chiefs running back – Kenneth Walker III.

"I ain't gonna lie I did," Emmanwori said. "I definitely did want to hold him under 100 [yards]. I don't really listen to all the media noise, but that was my motivation. I know a lot of dudes on the defense, that was their motivation, too, to stop him under 100 and play lights out on defense."

Going into the Week 7 "Sunday Night Football" game, the Seahawks hadn't allowed a 100-yard rusher in their last 35 games, including the playoffs. Walker, the reigning Super Bowl MVP, entered the matchup with his former team averaging more than 130 rushing yards per game.

'SNF' TAKEAWAYS: Is it time for a wide receiver to win an MVP?

In an apparent clash between unstoppable force and immovable object in prime time, the immovable object came away the clear winner. The Seahawks held Walker to 36 rushing yards on 14 attempts – the running back's worst game of the season.

"We put on a clinic," Emmanwori said before noting that the defense was disappointed the Chiefs narrowly avoided a shutout. "That was our goal, give them zero. We definitely could've accomplished that. But that just says what type of defense we are."

After the game, Walker refused to shake hands with any of his former teammates.

"(Expletive), we lost," Walker said about his cold shoulder approach, per multiple reports. "I was frustrated. That's about it. I [saw] them over there celebrating and (expletive). That's about it."

Seattle's next test will be shutting down the Chicago Bears' excellent offense on "Monday Night Football" in Week 8. No team is averaging more rushing yards per game than Chicago's 154.3.

Meanwhile, the Chiefs will look to bounce back after their first loss of the season. Their next matchup is on the road for a divisional battle against the Denver Broncos.

item.title: Jonathan Taylor: Trade rumors are out there, my wife discussing it doesn't change anything

item.content:encoded:
The Colts' decision to fire General Manager Chris Ballard last week has led to speculation about what other moves are coming for the team and particular attention has been paid to potential trades.

Running back Jonathan Taylor's name has come up in that speculation and he said last week that he hasn't given any thought to a move because his focus is on playing. Taylor's wife Ayanna doesn't have games to prepare for, however, and she made a couple of social media videos discussing the possibility of a trade over the weekend.

Those videos laid out the case for why the Colts would trade Taylor, including the lack of a 2027 first-round pick due to Ballard's trade for Sauce Gardner. After Sunday's 16-10 loss to the Vikings, Taylor was asked about those videos and he said he doesn't think his wife is only talking about things that already in the larger conversations surrounding the team.

“I think it’s been out there already, so I think her adding [to it] doesn’t really change anything,” Taylor said, via James Boyd of TheAthletic.com. “You know everybody’s on TikTok these days. So, you just have to come into work and stay focused.”

Taylor's teammates Quenton Nelson and DeForest Bucker have also seen their names come up in trade chatter and the only way that's likely to stop before November 10 is if the Colts is if they go ahead with moves involving all three players.

item.title: NFL kickers are 167-for-170 from inside 37 yards. Trey Smack had 2 of the 3 misses Sunday.
item.description: Once an NFL offense gets inside the 20-yard line, coming away with at least a field goal should be just about a sure thing.
item.content:encoded:
Once an NFL offense gets inside the 20-yard line, coming away with at least a field goal should be just about a sure thing. It wasn't for the Packers on Sunday in Detroit.

Packers kicker Trey Smack missed a 26-yard field goal wide right, and had a 35-yard field goal blocked, in the Packers' 20-17 loss to the Lions.

How rare is it for an NFL kicker to miss field goals that short? So far this season, NFL kickers are 167-for-170 on field goals from inside 37 yards. Smack had two of the three misses on Sunday, and the other was a 23-yarder by Bears kicker Cairo Santos that was blocked by the Vikings in Week 2.

The last time a kicker missed two field goals of 35 yards or shorter in the same game was seven years ago, when Patriots kicker Mike Nugent missed two in a game against the Browns. Nugent was cut afterward.

Packers coach Matt LaFleur says Smack won’t get cut. At least not yet. But it's safe to say Smack's seat is getting hot.

item.title: Ravens Report Card, Week 7: Recurring second-half issues apex in blowout loss
item.description: For the second straight week, the Ravens allowed zero first-half points and built up a double-digit lead, only to get shut out in the second half and lose. This time, the end result was worse, as the Ravens were outscored 35-0 over the final two quarters. Here are report card grades for the team’s offense […]
item.content:encoded:
For the second straight week, the Ravens allowed zero first-half points and built up a double-digit lead, only to get shut out in the second half and lose. This time, the end result was worse, as the Ravens were outscored 35-0 over the final two quarters.

Here are report card grades for the team’s offense and defense from a demoralizing Week 7 loss.

Quarterback: C-

Tyler Huntley’s final stat line is indicative of a solid performance, as he completed 68% percent of his 34 passes with over 300 total yards and a touchdown. However, after a few good drives in the first half, Huntley fizzled out as the game progressed. He was off-target on a fourth-down conversion throw and potential touchdown pass in the end zone. Huntley rushed only three times for 12 yards; his rushing prowess has strangely not been utilized much at all over the past few weeks.

Running Back: D+

Derrick Henry had his worst rushing output in recent memory against the Bengals, gaining only 45 yards on 17 attempts. Henry continues to find little running room behind the Ravens’ offensive line and has not appeared as decisive lately hitting holes and breaking tackles. He’s averaging only 3.9 yards per carry on the year now. Justice Hill had six touches for 33 scrimmage yards and Rasheen Ali got a few carries late in the game.

Wide Receiver: C+

Zay Flowers continues to excel despite the Ravens’ overall offensive struggles. He had one his best games of the season, totaling eight catches for 137 yards with a 48-yard touchdown on the first drive of the game. The rest of the wide receivers had minimal production. Rashod Bateman caught a pair of passes for 33 yards and Ja’Kobi Lane reeled in three receptions for 25 yards. Lane had a chance for a touchdown but the throw to him in the end zone was slightly too far outside.

Tight End: C-

For the second straight week, rookie Josh Cuevas was the leading receiver in the tight end room. He caught only two passes but gained 35 yards. Mark Andrews was targeted four times and caught three balls for 23 yards. Andrews has not exceeded 28 receiving yards in a game since Week 2 and also had another false start penalty in this game. Matthew Hibner returned from injury but was not a factor. Perhaps most concerning is the lack of notable blocking prowess the Ravens are getting from their tight ends. The offense definitely misses Pat Ricard and Charlie Kolar in the run game.

Offensive Line: D+

The Ravens cannot buy any injury luck on the offensive line. As soon as Cam Jurgens made his debut with the team, Vega Ioane suffered a knee injury early and did not return. The Ravens had multiple pre-snap penalties again from different offensive linemen and surrendered four sacks along with seven quarterback hits. Even more concerning than their pass protection consistencies is the group’s struggles in run blocking. The Bengals had one of the worst run defenses in the league entering this game and yet they completely shut down the Ravens’ rushing attack. The Ravens continue to get little push up front and no runs of 10+ yards were created in this game.

Defensive Line: D+

The Ravens were able to shut down a middling Bengals’ rushing attack, to the tune of just 73 yards on 20 carries (3.7 yards per carry). However, the Bengals were not looking to run the ball in the second half anyways when they trailed by 13 points. Baltimore’s defensive front did very little to impact the game in the second half from a pass rushing standpoint. Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones each finished with a pair of tackles and one quarterback hit, but Burrow had time to throw in the second half and picked the Ravens apart.

Edge Rusher: C-

The stage was set for Trey Hendrickson’s “revenge game” against his former team, but he had just one tackle with two quarterback hits. Hendrickson and the rest of the edge rusher group was not much of a factor versus Joe Burrow. Mike Green did have one nice sack and a tackle-for-loss, but Zion Young’s production continues to be a little underwhelming. This was the Ravens’ first game without Tavius Robinson and his absence was felt.

Linebacker: D+

Impact plays from the Ravens’ linebacker group were not prevalent in this game. Roquan Smith and Trenton Simpson combined for 14 tackles, but they each recorded no tackles for loss, quarterback hits or sacks. Smith had a chance to make a pass breakup or interception on a pass attempt over the middle but was beaten for a catch instead. The linebackers evidently did a good job bottling up the run, but they were party to some of the struggles in pass coverage as well.

Cornerback: D

It was a difficult second-half performance for Marlon Humphrey, who missed multiple tackles that resulted in big gains. Humphrey and Nate Wiggins both struggled defending the Bengals’ star wide receivers. Tee Higgins dominated the Ravens for 148 yards on six catches with a touchdown and had a long 44-yard reception. Ja’Marr Chase only had 62 yards but scored a touchdown and ripped off a lot of yards after the catch.

Safety: D+

Kyle Hamilton had one big tackle for loss on a third-and-short rushing attempt. Aside from that, there weren’t many successful plays from the safeties at all. Hamilton uncharacteristically missed multiple tackles including one at the goal line where the Bengals then scored. Malaki Starks did the same. With Jaylinn Hawkins sidelined, backups K’Von Wallace and Keondre Jackson both played expanded roles. Wallace had four tackles and a quarterback hit.

Special Teams: C

Tyler Loop bounced back in this game by making both of his field goal tries, albeit they were each 34 yards or shorter. Ryan Eckley was effective punting with three punts for 145 yards. LaJohntay Wester did not return any of the Bengals’ four punts The Ravens have not received many explosive plays in the return game this year.

item.title: NFC West Recap: 49ers’ lead shrinks to two; Seahawks, Rams both win
item.description: Seahawks and Rams both just have to win when the 49ers lose.
item.content:encoded:
6-1.

The unbeaten run is over. The San Francisco 49ers lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons, and they did it in the most 49ers way possible: three turnovers, a missed extra point, and a parade of defensive penalties on the drive that decided it. Yes, they were injured and a loss was expected, but it was a brutal display of errors they simply couldn’t afford to make. Taking it one step further, even with backups, they were very uncharacteristic errors on top of it.

To make matters worse, the 49ers special teams picked a bad time to remember they were 49ers special teams, with some atrocious kickoff coverage letting the Falcons start with good field position.

It started fine. Running back Christian McCaffrey ripped off chunks on a 10-play opening touchdown drive, and when a thigh injury sent him to the sideline, rookie running back Kaelon Black ran in a 30-yard touchdown for a 14-3 lead. His first touchdown, mind you.

Then the giveaways started, the 49ers’ lead was blown, and anything bad that could happen, pretty much did.

After all the gifts, 29-20. The 49ers go into the bye up two games over the Seattle Seahawks, and desperately need to get healthy.

Seattle Seahawks (4-3)

The Seattle Seahawks beat embarrassed the Kansas City Chiefs 20-3 on Sunday Night Football. That leaves the Minnesota Vikings as the lone undefeated team.

After two straight losses (which we, as 49ers fans, enjoyed), the Seahawks smothered Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who threw for 165 yards and an interception. Kansas City never reached the red zone.

Sam Darnold forgot he was Sam Darnold and went 20-of-28 for 257 yards passing with a touchdown and an interception, and not a single sack. Running back Emanuel Wilson also notched his first 100-yard game as a Seahawk against the Kansas City defense.

However, a bill is coming in injuries. Wide receiver Rashid Shaheed (knee) and running back Velus Jones Jr. (hamstring) were ruled out, and left tackle Charles Cross was rolled up on in the fourth quarter.

To add insult to the Chiefs, running back Kenneth Walker, who left the Seahawks in the offseason for the Chiefs and was a sleeper MVP pick this year, got only 36 yards on 14 carries. Basically, Walker was doing what the Seahawks had been struggling to do up until this game: run the ball.

And thus, the Seahawks begin digging themselves out of the hole.

Arizona Cardinals (2-5)

The Arizona Cardinals put Larry Fitzgerald in their Ring of Honor and retired his No. 11 at halftime. Nice of the Denver Broncos to bring enough fans to make it feel like a road game. It was more Denver than it was Arizona, which is probably what you get as Arizona when you go into the game 2-4.

Then there was the actual game. A game Denver won 30-16. Arizona gave up a 62-yard touchdown run to quarterback Bo Nix and a 52-yard screen touchdown to running back R.J. Harvey, and the Broncos tied their season high in points.

Tight end Trey McBride caught 10 passes for 111 yards receiving and the Cardinals’ first touchdown in over 100 game minutes. Yes, you read that right: 100 game minutes. Congrats to McBride. Running back Bam Knight averaged nearly seven yards per carry. Those highlights aren’t going to matter because the Cardinals who marched for a walk-off win in Los Angeles last week couldn’t finish anything here. The Cardinals went 1-for-5 in the red zone, and they’re 12-of-28 on the season.

If you really want a single drive that can recap this game, just look to the final drive: five snaps inside the 1-yard line thanks to Denver penalties, a sack back to the 5, and nothing on fourth down.

I don’t think 49ers fans need to worry about the Cardinals this year…

Los Angeles Rams (3-4)

The Los Angeles Rams are no longer in last place. It’s not quite “Ram-ing” it, but going to third place is certainly progress. They beat the Las Vegas Raiders 35-21, and it was closer than that sounds—at least in the fourth quarter when the Raiders managed 15 points and their first two touchdowns.

Quarterback Matthew Stafford threw three first-half touchdowns, and running back Kyren Williams added one on the ground for a 28-6 halftime lead. Then the Rams did Rams things. Las Vegas converted a fake punt. Williams fumbled. Running back Blake Corum’s touchdown run came back on a facemask. Stafford threw an interception when tight end Colby Parkinson popped the ball into the air. Corum finally put it away late with a rushing score.

Special teams, turnovers, penalties: the same problems that have followed this team all season. They just won anyway. The Raiders, meanwhile, are starting to remember they are the Raiders. This was not the game we wanted them to remember that detail.

Onto Week 8

The 49ers are on bye. This means Christian McCaffrey’s thigh also gets a bye. It also means that we can do something else on Sunday. So, bye.

The Seahawks host the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football. The Bears had quite a Thursday Night Football game, beating the New England Patriots 30-24. Playing on Thursday night gives them extra rest before they travel to Seattle. If anyone can get the 49ers’ three-game lead back, it’s da Bears. Do it for Ditka.

The Cardinals travel to face the Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys are doing NFC East things on Monday Night Football, but sit at 2-4 as of this writing. The NFC East hasn’t been anything special lately, and that shouldn’t change after Monday. It wouldn’t be surprising to see a Cardinals win here.

The Rams host the Los Angeles Chargers in the battle for Levi’s South housesitters SoFi Stadium. The Chargers have failed to win a game yet this season, so maybe Jim Harbaugh and company can get their first victory over the Rams. The last thing 49ers fans want is to have the Rams crawling back into this, so there’s a three-way battle for the division. Please Chargers?

1st:San Francisco 49ers; Next: BYE
2nd:Seattle Seahawks; Next: vs. Chicago Bears (Monday Night Football)
3rd:Los Angeles Rams; Next: vs. Los Angeles Chargers
4th:Arizona Cardinals; Next: at Dallas Cowboys

item.title: Bengals News: Statement Win Vs. Ravens
item.description: The Bengals weren’t going down without a fight, but it turned into them mauling the Ravens instead.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals sure know how to irritate their fan base. In their win against the Baltimore Ravens, the team looked absolutely terrible. The offense was disjointed and the defense kept giving up explosive plays, especially on 3rd-and-long.

Ultimately that script flipped at half time. The team walked right down the field with Joe Burrow being as surgical as we know he can. It culminated in a perfectly lofted ball to Mike Gesicki. The offense would do that four more times in a row to score 35 points in the second half, which would be enough to win the game.

It was one of the more dominant offensive performances we have seen in quite some time, and that is the biggest reason Cincinnati fans get frustrated by an offense sort of running in place. They are capable of doing this kind of thing anytime the Bengals get an offensive possession. Obviously it is impossible to expect them to score every drive, but they’ve shown they are capable of scoring serious points.

You got to feel bad for Cousins. He will almost certainly be benched after the team dropped four straight games after starting 3-0.
